#1093. 1966 World Cup hero Sir Geoff Hurst backs Mail's dementia carers appeal after six of his England team-mates developed the disease

Published: 17:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 17:59 EST, 16 November 2026

World Cup hero Sir Geoff Hurst has thrown his support behind the Daily Mail’s dementia carers appeal.

Sir Geoff, who saw six of his England team-mates suffer from dementia before they died, is now the sole survivor of Sir Alf Ramsey’s 1966 trophy-winning team.

Manchester United legend Sir Bobby Charlton and his elder brother Jack Charlton of Leeds United lived with the condition in their later years.

So did Martin Peters, who scored a goal alongside Sir Geoff’s famous hat-trick to beat West Germany 4-2 in the 1966 World Cup final at Wembley Stadium.

Dementia also hit Ray Wilson, of Everton, Sir Geoff’s strike partner Roger Hunt, of Liverpool, and Manchester United midfielder Nobby Stiles.

Six out of the 11 England players who started in the World Cup final 60 years ago developing the disease is a startling ratio, and has driven home research linking heading the ball to degenerative brain conditions in later life.

World Cup hero Sir Geoff Hurst has thrown his support behind the Daily Mail’s dementia carers appeal

Sir Geoff has become a staunch advocate of Alzheimer’s Society and vowed to back the Mail’s appeal, delivered in partnership with Alzheimer’s Society and the Mail Force charity, to raise millions towards a nationwide support network for millions of people across Britain caring for friends and family members with dementia.

He said: ‘As always, I am supporting Alzheimer’s Society in this endeavour. Several of my colleagues suffered and are still suffering in some cases this disease and the more we can do to research it, for better things will be in the long run hopefully.

‘So, let’s get behind this Alzheimer’s campaign to help the families of those are suffering and do as much good as possible.’

The Mail’s new Dementia Carers Together appeal passed its first target of raising £100,000 in just a week, enough to pay for nearly 3,000 places on new classes to give carers vital support and information about their rights and the services available to them.

The six-week courses will allow attendees to meet others in a similar situation and help to address the loneliness, exhaustion and overwhelming responsibilities many face following a loved one’s diagnosis.

The appeal has already won the backing of every major political party leader, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying: ‘Just a little bit of help can make something feel bearable or doable that without it, would all of a sudden just overwhelm somebody.’

The family of Ray Wilson, England’s left back in 1966, are also supporting the Mail’s campaign.

Wilson died in 2018 at the age of 83 after years with Alzheimer’s disease, during most of which time he was cared for by his devoted wife Pat and their family.

His daughter-in-law, Linda Wilson, said: ‘It’s really good campaign. It would be nice to have a six-week programme available to everybody regardless of where they are in the country and not reliant upon some sort of postcode lottery.

‘Pat was always lucky because Ray would go to a Help the Aged day centre in Slaithwaite twice a week and it gave her some respite.

Dementia Carers Together is raising money to fund new courses across the UK to give tens of thousands of struggling unpaid dementia carers vital emotional and practical support.

For further information, visit dailymail.com/dementia

Online: Visit justgiving.com/campaign/mailforce

By Text: To donate £10, text CARER to 70115. To donate £20, text LOVE to 70115. To donate £30, text HEART to 70115. Texts will cost your donation amount plus your network charge.

By phone: Call 0300 1234577. Standard charges may apply.

By cheque: Send cheques made payable to Mail Force Charity to:

Dementia Carers Together, 42 Phoenix Court, Hawkins Road, Colchester CO2 8JY

‘Having support and knowing where to go and look for it is important. You feel shellshocked when you get the diagnosis. You feel quite alone and wondering what’s going to happen and how fast.

‘So much of the care is patient centred but the people supporting the patient need support as well.’

Wilson’s widow Pat died last year, and the family are on a fundraising mission of their own, selling the drawings done by Ray after his diagnosis with proceeds set to be donated to the Alzheimer’s Society.

He had never shown any inclination to draw but one day at the breakfast table picked up a biro and started to sketch on the inside of a cereal box, and hardly ever stopped, producing hundreds of drawings which Pat kept after he died.

A small number bear Wilson’s signature, some refer to his footballing past at Huddersfield and Everton.

Sky Sports presenter Hayley McQueen’s father Gordon McQueen, the former Leeds, Manchester United and Scotland centre half, died in 2023 at the age of 70 after a long struggle with vascular dementia.

She is also throwing her support behind the Dementia Carers Together appeal to make a difference for the families of those suffering from the disease.

She said: ‘I’m backing this campaign with the Alzheimer’s Society who’ve been incredibly helpful with my family throughout the battle that we had with my dad and also going through unfortunately another Alzheimer’s situation close to home.

‘I lost both my grandparents so I understand the burden of trying to care for loved ones and family members not knowing where you’re going to get help. So, please get behind this campaign and please note that you’re not going through this alone.’

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the mid-2000s, Freddy Adu was earmarked as the next big thing in world football.

After making his professional debut as a 14-year-old for D.C. United in 2004, he became the youngest ever player to appear in professional sports in the United States. His international debut came at the age of 16, amid reported interest from some of Europe’s biggest clubs.

But the career that followed was a nomadic one, as his progress stalled and Adu would turn into something of a globetrotter in search of fresh opportunities.

This saw the American take in stints in Portugal, France, Greece and Serbia amongst other places, but Adu believes that a key issue with his career was the fact that these teams were often more interested in the marketing buzz that signing him would generate, rather than handing him opportunities on the pitch.

“I’d sign for teams, then you’d find out they were just trying to use you for the marketing part of it, to get eyeballs on their team,” Adu tells FourFourTwo.

“Then when you’re not playing for that team, it’s like ‘Why am I here? I’m living in a different country, I’m trying to get my career going and I’m not getting a chance to play’.

“At some point, you just figure out ‘This isn’t going to work out’.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For Adu, the mixed messages from clubs he signed for would prove to be extremely frustrating at times when he was looking to get his career back on track.

|There were so many different places where the front office wanted you, but the coach had different ideas,” he adds. “I’d been brought in under false pretences.

“Then you go to another team, sometimes you’re playing and it works out at the start, but then it doesn’t work out.

“After a while, it wasn’t fun any more, you start losing confidence in yourself, like ‘How am I here, and how am I not getting a chance to play here?’ You start questioning the reasons why you were brought in.”

For Adu, this cycle began in 2008, when Monaco brought him in initially on loan from Benfica for the 2008/09 season, before declining to make the move permanent at the end of that campaign.

“The whole thing started when I was in Monaco – the president wanted to bring me in, I knew him, I was cool with him, but the coach had different ideas.”

Unai Emery’s side will be relieved that they took a maximum nine points from their opening three games as their fixtures in this competition are getting a lot harder. This away game in Barcelona is followed up by a tricky trip to Turkey. Then it is tough back-to-back home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund.

Unai Emery has managed more than 1,100 matches but will never forget the drama of “La Remontada” as he returns to the scene on Tuesday night.

Emery is back at the Nou Camp in the Champions League for the first time since one of the most epic games in the history of the competition. While in charge of Paris St-Germain nine years ago, Emery took his team to Barcelona with a 4-0 lead from the round-of-16 first leg. Yet he was left stunned as Barcelona recovered to win the rematch 6-1, with three goals in the final seven minutes and the winner proving hugely controversial.

Sergi Roberto’s goal five minutes into added time caused a massive backlash as PSG claimed it was offside, with Emery claiming on Monday that the match showed that VAR was “necessary”.

Honking weather here in Barcelona with the rain hammering down at the Nou Camp.

It has been forecast all day and until about 5pm Spanish time it did appear that the predictions were wrong.

No such luck, however, and it is pretty torrential at the moment. Football updates to follow.

Aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

Team news from Nou Camp to follow shortly.

The Liverpool legend succeeded Joe Fagan in the Anfield dugout

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By 1985, Kenny Dalglish had already established himself as an all-time Liverpool great.

But after eight years as being the Reds’ talismanic force on the pitch, Dalglish was handed the opportunity to play an even bigger role at the club, when he was asked to succeed manager Joe Fagan.

While Dalglish would excel in his new dual player-manager position, it was not a role he had expected to take on, but he admits he was unable to refuse the offer.

“I don't know why the club asked me to become player-manager in 1985,” the Scot tells FourFourTwo.

“But they did, so I said, ‘OK, no problem for me. If that's what you want, I'll have a go.’”

For Dalglish, it was the structure and culture of the club that made what would be a daunting transition more manageable.

“The people around me were important – there was a vast experience in that dressing room, with the coaching staff, and Bob Paisley came back to help,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“He was fantastic. The people upstairs, the chief executive, they'd do all the negotiations for wages and transfers, I didn't want to be involved in money. It was really well organised.”

This backing from everyone in the club allowed Dalglish to focus on the on-pitch matters.

“They said, ‘All you can do is be your best' – to come out of the dressing room and sit in the manager's office, those were my team-mates and it was tough at times, but it wasn't something that you could turn down,” he adds.

And Dalglish’s best would prove to be more than good enough, as he would win the first of three league titles as manager of Liverpool in that very first season in his new role.

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1080. Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure. Researchers found that these animals carry roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood on average — similar to the levels of plastics found in humans — with the highest levels found in those that lived closest to urban areas and waste-management facilities. The findings are an important step to better understand how these particles impact wildlife, says geochemist Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou.

Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences. The tool, announced on 11 November, has already impressed researchers. Its underlying AI model was trained on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. But the tool can also make predictions when fed data from cell types that it wasn’t trained on, which could help researchers more quickly identify variants underlying disease, says DeepMind scientist Adam Gayoso.

An approach that measures waist circumference and focuses on excess body fat could be a more accurate way to diagnose obesity — and identify people with related health risks — than body mass index (BMI). In an analysis of data from more than 800,000 people, researchers found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The new framework classified an extra 5–9% of people as having obesity, who would have been labelled only as overweight with the BMI-based approach.

Bioengineered bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form for plants could replace up to half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, slashing the greenhouse-gas emissions associated with these chemicals, researchers suggest. Bacteria can deliver nitrogen to roots more efficiently than synthetic fertilizers, and scientists are engineering them to feed nitrogen to crop plants that don’t have natural microbial partners, such as maize and wheat. Gene-edited biofertilizers have already been used in the United States, but a slew of advances are needed to demonstrate higher levels of nitrogen fixation.

In July, artificial-intelligence titan Anthropic acquired a biotechnology company that developed two promising drug leads with just one full-time human employee and an AI assistant. The mini-firm benefited from the help of several part-time consultants and external research organizations to craft its products — two early-stage antibodies designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy — and many more researchers will be required to take the drugs forward. But the acquisition has sparked discussion about whether one-person, AI-enabled biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future.

With the rise of multidisciplinary science and artificial intelligence, biologists are “poised to at last understand the complexity of life”, writes epigeneticist Edith Heard, chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London. But people are what will unlock these discoveries, not technology alone. “Funders, institutions and scientific leaders must embrace new technologies while protecting the conditions in which discovery thrives: curiosity, collaboration and, above all, the freedom and support to follow unexpected observations to see where they lead,” Heard writes.

“Environmental change is altering the conditions in which brains develop and minds are sustained”, says a new report from a commission convened by Nature Mental Health. For example, heat, air and noise pollution and loss of green space have been linked with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline — with poorer people, children and older people among those most exposed. The Earth–Brain–Health Commission offers a new framework for uniting neuroscience, psychiatry, public health and environmental science around shared challenges and solutions.

Nature Mental Health editorial | 6 min read

Get the gist in the accompanying policy brief (9 min read)

Reference: Nature Mental Health Earth–Brain–Health Commission report

The lawless simulated world of blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) — which is just about to release its sixth iteration — offers researchers an intricately crafted testbed for road-safety experiments, says computer scientist Julius Schöning. (BBC | 7 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x

Today I’m adding M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything to my reading list. The post-apocalyptic novel was announced as the winner of this year’s Booker prize on 9 November — the first “bona fide” science-fiction novel to win the award, says Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation.

Let me know what other science-fiction books I should add to the pile, along with your feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

After six years in Italy and Scotland, Paul Gascoigne returned to English football in March 1998 when he signed for Middlesbrough.

At this stage of his career, Gazza was no longer the force of nature that lit up Italia 90 and Euro 96 as he body struggled to keep up the pace with his footballing brain.

However, his ability to be at the centre of attention and to entertain all around him, remained undiminished.

Former Boro goalkeeper Mark Schwarzer had a front row seat for all of Gazza’s pranks and hijinks - whether they lit up the dressing room, or left team-mates seeing red.

“Gazza has a heart of gold,” Schwarzer tells FourFourTwo. “All he wants to do is make people laugh, have fun and bring smiles to people’s faces.

“He’d do stuff that was outrageously funny and wrong, but there was never any malice.”

When Gascoigne arrived at the Riverside Stadium, he joined from Rangers at the tail end of a campaign which had seen him score just three goals in 28 games and while his impact had clearly diminished from his early ‘90s pomp, it was clear to Schwarzer that the ability was still there.

The kit, which combines a white base with black sleeves and neon yellow detailing, was worn for the first time in Saturdayâs 2-0 Bundesliga win over Heidenheim.

But instead of excitement, its debut was met with anger in the stands and online. Fans unfurled banners blasting it as âthe cruelest jersey in the leagueâ while chants of âWe want black and yellow jerseysâ rang out before kick-off, a pointed reminder of the clubâs traditional colours.

Across social media, the reaction was no kinder. Many supporters branded the design a betrayal of Dortmundâs historic identity, with critics arguing it looks more like a training top than a shirt fit for the famous Schwarzgelben.

Managing director Carsten Cramer took personal responsibility for the fallout, telling reporters: "The criticism has been received, and we are addressing it. The responsibility lies with me. We won't always be able to please everyone when selecting jerseys."

Sporting director Sebastian Kehl was more measured, reminding fans that opinions on kit design are always split.

"I think we have different opinions about jerseys every year," he said. "It will never be the case that a Borussia Dortmund jersey meets with 100 percent approval. Fundamentally, we know which colors represent our city and our club, and that this is reflected in the design of almost all jerseys."

He added, with a touch of humour: "However, there are also people who want something younger, something fresh, something creative. The new jersey brought BVB three points in Heidenheim. A successful jersey, I'd say. Everything else is a discussion that we as a club consider normal."

Whether the kit makes another appearance when Dortmund travel to Mainz on September 27 remains to be seen, but if it does, you best believe that Dortmund fans to have something to say about it.

#1070. Liverpool calamity hands Iraola his most chastening night yet

Andoni Iraola looked up to the ceiling of Fenerbahce’s media auditorium as he tried to find the words to describe the madness he had just witnessed.

“Cheap” was his first conclusion, swiftly followed by “messy”; technically, Liverpool’s head coach was right but this was a moment when nobody would have found issue had he gone further. “Absurd” and “preposterous” would have been more accurate portrayals of this calamity.

Liverpool have won two European trophies in Istanbul, but they do not tend to enjoy visits to Turkey. Roy Hodgson, in August 2010, was the last Anfield manager to oversee a win here and there was an irony that the hero of that night in Trabzon – Dirk Kuyt – masterminded this downfall.

Kuyt, interim head coach, got a remarkable response out of a Fenerbahce team who had amassed 1,086 Premier League appearances between them and he was as giddy as the locals after Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown and substitute Vedat Muriqi scored to give the club a famous night.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#1062. RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liam Drew is a freelance science journalist based near London.

Protection against the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) must expand to lower-income countries, which are harder hit.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty

“Something’s wrong with the data. There are too few people in hospitals” with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), epidemiologist Caroline Klint Johannesen recalls a colleague remarking while analysing Danish health records for last winter.

On 1 October 2025, Denmark introduced a nationwide policy of vaccinating pregnant people against RSV — a respiratory pathogen that usually causes mild symptoms but can lead to severe disease and even death in vulnerable people, including infants and older adults. Maternal antibodies induced by the vaccine cross the placenta to protect babies for around the first six months of their lives, when they are most at risk. Newborns at high risk of severe disease, including premature infants, whose mothers had not been vaccinated, were given injections of monoclonal antibodies.

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

Johannesen, a vaccine researcher at Nordsjællands Hospital in Hillerød, Denmark, found1 that infant hospital admissions plummeted. The immunizations are working, she says (see ‘Newborn protection’).

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that every year, RSV hospitalizes roughly 3.6 million and kills about 100,000 children under 5 years old. Of these deaths, 97% occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

The virus is also dangerous to older adults — although those risks are widely underappreciated by both physicians and the public. Historically, testing has been sparse, and there are no global statistics for RSV-related adult deaths. But over the age of 60, hospitalizations and mortality increase with age, especially in people with other diseases such as chronic heart and lung conditions. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that between around 10,000 and 25,000 people have died in each of the past two winters, especially in older age groups.

Since 2022, when European regulators approved nirsevimab — a long-acting monoclonal antibody against RSV — a second antibody and three vaccines have been developed for use in adults, one of which is suitable for pregnant people.

“It’s just remarkable,” says Buddy Creech, a paediatrician at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, to have gone “from no mechanism to prevent RSV to an embarrassment of riches”. Dozens of countries across Europe, Asia and North and South America have launched various immunization programmes.

Published: 17:56 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 19:19 EST, 16 November 2026

Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz scored a stunning brace for Germany as Jurgen Klopp's side thumped the Netherlands in the Nations League.

The 23-year-old has had a tough time of it at Anfield since his £116million move to the club last summer, but has never really struggled on the international stage.

And he continued that trend on Monday evening with two goals for his side to help them top their Nations League group.

His first was the pick of the bunch. Wirtz moved along the forward line as a Dutch side without Virgil van Dijk struggled to contain him. He picked up the ball around 25 yards out, cut inside onto his weaker left foot, and curled a pearling effort into the far corner off the post.

That goal, which came on the hour mark, put his side 2-0 up after Freiburg's Derry Scherhant had scored the opener, and Wirtz wasn't done there.

Centre back Nico Schlotterbeck made it 3-0 before the Liverpool man picked up his second of the night after drifting into the penalty box unmarked and finishing high after good work from Brajan Gruda.

Cette version de Wirtz avec le maillot de la Mannschaft c’est celle qu’on aimerait voir chaque semaine en PL. Quel missile pour faire le break ! Meilleur buteur allemand sur cette édition de l’UNL. 🇩🇪🔥 pic.twitter.com/m0DqaOungS

Florian Wirtz scored a brace for Germany as they thumped the Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League action

Liverpool midfielder Wirtz received a big hug from a smiling Jurgen Klopp at full time

Gruda himself, who is on loan at RB Leipzig from Brighton, wrapped up the five-star win on a night that arguably saw Klopp announce himself as Germany boss.

After full-time, the ex-Liverpool manager gave Wirtz a huge hug as the duo beamed with big smiles on their faces.

While it was a night to remember for Germany, a Netherlands team that included the likes of Micky van de Ven, Jurrien Timber and Wirtz's Liverpool team-mate Cody Gakpo were left exasperated.

Van Dijk had pulled out of the squad with a knock after playing with a knock in recent weeks.

His side will still, though, compete in the Nations League quarter-finals after finishing second in the group, finishing ahead of Greece on goal difference.

As for Wirtz, he will hope his performance will help continue what has been an uphill climb so far this season.

He also found the net for Germany in their first match of the international break – a 3-1 win over Serbia – and picked up a goal and assist in Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace before the international break.

In total, he has two goals and five assists in 15 games for Liverpool this season – though the Reds will hope those numbers increase as the season goes on.

His second goal came as he drifted into the penalty area and finished high into the net

Last month, meanwhile, Reds manager Andoni Iraola insisted he has full faith in his midfielder.

'I think he has had a little bit of everything this season,' he said. 'He has had good games, probably the other day was not his best game, especially offensively. We trust Florian.

'Florian is a very good player. He was coming from good performances in the international break, I think. I think it is a matter of everyone to find his moment.'

Klopp hailed him 'exceptional', meanwhile, during the last international break.

#1058. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

What a finish from Viktor Gyökeres from a tight angle 📐🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/EET5P7aJ2X

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

Cherki wastes an opportunity to pass to an unmarked Haaland in the box by trying and failing to force his shot though Orban’s legs. Khusanov has to make a foul to stop a Leipzig break.

Doku blazes a shot over to end a City break after Donnarumma had caught a cross following the free-kick.

Leipzig have a free-kick on the left after a daft Allan foul on Banzuzi. Three more minutes to come.

Terrific save from Vandevooort low to his left, almost clawing it back from behind him with a Stretch Armstrong left arm after Doku’s cross kicked up and struck Haaland’s leg.

Gruda rolls the ball into an empty net after deceiving Donnarumma but both knew he was a mile offside when Gomis’s pass found him.

Haaland hits the post with a right-foot shot from an offside position after either jumping the gun or, more likely, Cherki delaying the pass too long.

Now Cherki thunders a left-foot shot into the crossbar after a good work from Kovacic.

City have to go all the way back to Donnarumma after Banzuzi heads Fernández’s inswinging corner back to him.

City corner on the left after O’Reilly’s underlapping run catches Leipzig on the back foot.

The left winger plays a one-two with Cherki, the No 10 giving the ball back with a backheel, then crosses to the back post. Fernández can only reach it at the apex of his jump with the crown of his head and Ndiaye can’t stop it going out for a goalkick.

Enzo, not for the first time, goes down clutching his face when brushed by an opponent’s hand. The crowd whistles him as he does his dying fly act.

Golden chance for Haaland when Cherki’s pass ricochets off Banzuzi to the centre-forward by the penalty spot. He strikes it first time with his right foot but Vandervoort is equal to it, swooping low to his left to keep it out with a strong left wrist.

Some bright moments for the home side who are overplaying in attack much as Arshavin-era Arsenal used to do. City have looked good on the break but have failed to exploit Haaland’s channel running and ability to ghost away from Orban and Lukeba with the right pass.

Leipzig trying to send a message to the fans with his half-time playlist: I Will Survive and Don’t Stop Believing so far.

Baku is booked for scything down O’Reilly who had laid the ball off long before Baku dived in.

Gruda butchers a very good chance on the right of the City box after Fernandez and Cherki are caught upfield and leave Anderson minding the shop all alone. Baku, coming round Gruda, was screaming for the lay-up to shoot but Gruda took it on himself and scuffed it tamely wide.

Anderson is a foul magnet. Opponents keep catching and clipping him.

Baumgartner heeds the crowd’s advice and has a pop from 25 yards with a right-foot curling effort that doesn’t bend back in sufficiently. Donnarumma paid it the compliment of a full-length dive to his left but it was never on target.

Leipzig are guilty of overelaboration in and around the City box. Too many tricks and flicks, not enough shots and crosses. Haaland is giving his team-mates some jip for not reading his runs.

Cherki pings a pass out to Enzo on the right and he slips as he tries to cross, his momentum as he fell forcing the cross deeper than he had planned and it sails beyond a visibly frustrated Haaland who keeps making good runs but has yet to be found.

City are dicing with danger by letting Nusa run at them from positions on both wings and through the middle. They manage to stop him threading ir flicking passes through to Romulo twice in the space of 30 seconds but it would be less stressful to cut it off at source further away from their goal.

City can’t hang on to the ball in high areas, yielding possession too cheaply and Leipzig swarm forward down the right with City scrambling back. When the cut-back is played into the box, it is behind the first wave of Leipzig runners but galloping behind is Raum, the cavalry. He gets there and crashes a shot with his left that is blocked.

A replay of Donnarumma’s ‘save’ show that it was on target and the keeper could easily have squirted it through his hands into the goal. Small wonder he rotated his head as if auditioning for a part in the Exorcist to look back in relief.

Leipzig take the corner short and City push them back and try to start a counter that ends when Baumgartner takes Anderson out with a rash sliding tackle that upends the England midfielder.

Nusa, who has licence to roam, pops up on the right wing and cuts inside past Guéhi, dribbling across the 18-yard line before thumping a rising shot that Donnarumma puts his hands above his hands to catch but doesn’t cling on. Haaland, who hasn’t had a kick, closes the keeper Vandevoort down from his blindside and he flaps at his clearance, ballooning it straight tp Foden, 30 yards from goal. Banzuzi makes sure Foden doesn’t make them pay.

Leipzig break at pace with O’Reilly caught upfield, switching it to their left and running 50 yards towards the City box but Nunes makes an impressive recovery run to win the tackle.

Anderson almost picks up out O’Reilly who had made an underlapping run down the left as Ndiaye lured Baku out to the wing. But Orban stops O’Reilly spinning on to the pass.

Ndiaye rides his luck and two tackles before the ball just skips away form him as he was closing towards the 18-yard line but Leipzig botch the clearance and Foden feeds a lovely pass in from the right to Cherki who opens his body and wraps a left-foot shot the wrong side of the left post.

Cherki intercepts a pass meant for Nusa but goes backwards instead of looking for Foden down the right, killing the impetus of an unexpected interception.

Nusa stretches his legs down the left after a clumsy lay-off from Cherki and shifts the ball inside to meet Romulo’s run between Khusanov and Nunes but Nunes sticks with him and forces him deep, so close to the byline in fact that his attempt to square it goes straight to Donnarumma.

Khusanov, under pressure from Romulo, squeezes a pass that deflects off him and goes out for a City throw-in.

After a moment’s silence for Jesús de Miguel who was killed after being injured while playing for Tenerife earlier this week, Manchester City kick off, attacking from left to right. They are in black with yellow trim, the colours of the bee emblem of the city of Manchester. Leipzig are in white with red bits. City move the ball back to Donnarumma who instigates and attack up the left that the home side deals with easily and when they try again Baku heads Nunes’ long ball away.

City only have a small portion of the stadium for travelling support – but the boos for the Champions League anthem is heard loud and clear. There are a few fans dressed up as sheikhs too.

We know each other very well and we’re almost like brothers. I know his philosophy and how he wants to play. Enzo is a winner and he’ll be looking to win trophies with Manchester City.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

Rangnick's men are depleted but home advantage could see them edge this one.

#1054. Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

An MRI scan of the basal ganglia, seen here in section and colour-coded.Credit: Zephyr/SPL

The basal ganglia are groups of cells that sit deep in the brain and process motor, cognitive, mood and decision-making information. They are linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions from Parkinson’s and Huntington’s disease to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and addiction.

Now, researchers have published the world’s most-detailed atlas of basal ganglia so far, comprising 25.5 million brain cells from humans, macaques and marmosets. The work is described in a collection of 26 papers published in Cell, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, Cell Genomics and Neuron. The research includes understudied neurons1, provides insights about how some brain cells change with age2 and suggests which might be linked to diseases3.

The atlas, a collaboration between hundreds of scientists in nine countries, is part of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) — a US$500-million project launched in 2022 by the US National Institutes of Health aimed at creating reference maps of mammalian brains.

“It’s a massive dictionary that we needed in the field,” says Ana Muñoz-Manchado, a neuroscientist at the University of Cádiz in Spain, who studies the basal ganglia in neurodegenerative disorders.

The basal ganglia atlas contains 21 million cells from the brains of six humans, three million cells from three rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, and 1.5 million cells from two marmosets4. The researchers also used data from previously published maps of the whole mouse brain5,6.

By comparing the basal ganglia between the primate species, the researchers identified 61 cell types in humans, macaques and marmosets that have been conserved over 76 million years3.

The team analysed brain tissue samples from different developmental stages across the lifespan of the species. The latest work combines information about these cells in unprecedented detail, from measurements of their gene expression and DNA modifications that control gene regulation to recordings of their electrical activity, as well as how DNA is folded inside their nuclei.

The researchers also mapped where each cell is located in the brain and designed a common framework to characterize and annotate the cells. It is “essentially a scaffold on which we can now fairly readily complete the rest of the brain”, explains Michael Hawrylycz, a bioinformatician at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who took part in the project.

One study examined 1.1 million cells in the basal ganglia’s largest structure — known as the striatum — from 19 deceased human donors7. Unlike many other brain areas, the striatum has no neat anatomical boundaries. The researchers identified six zones in the human and macaque striatum that had distinct molecular signatures, each containing distinct populations of neurons and glial cells.

“The cells in these zones all look the same under the microscope, but have very strong transcriptional differences and are strikingly consistent from person to person,” said co-author Evan Macosko, a neurobiologist at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in a press release from the institute.

Macosko and his colleagues also found that gene expression patterns that distinguished each zone from the other became increasingly similar with age, particularly in brain regions affected by Huntington’s or Parkinson’s disease.

Another study analysed nearly four million cells in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from 178 deceased adult donors aged from 27 to more than 902. The researchers found that the cellular make-up of the two brain regions varied between people, particularly for non-neuronal cells known as glial cells. This underscores the need for brain cell atlases to account for these individual differences.

Only formed in 1999, the club have used innovative thinking to become perennial title contenders – FFT headed to see them host rivals FC Copenhagen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Beneath gathering rain clouds and surrounded by thousands of hectares of windswept heathland, FourFourTwo is staring at a 33-foot statue of Vladimir Lenin.

We're not in St Petersburg or Minsk – or any former Soviet nation, for that matter – but Denmark's Jutland peninsula, as it begins to drizzle with rain. It's so wild and remote that old Vlad is one of the few faces we've seen since arriving this morning. Much like the Russian revolutionary – carved in bronze, suspended in mid-air and lying flat on his back, just like at his Moscow mausoleum – we're beginning to wonder what the hell we're doing here.

“We like to imagine that Lenin is contemplating all the terrible things he did in life,” explains Birgitte Damgaard, the proprietor of the land the statue now calls home. Birgitte's father, a local textiles tycoon and art collector, vowed to rescue the statue after watching television footage of it being toppled by Latvians during the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. “It was brought more than 500 miles – first by truck, then by ship,” she tells FFT, after we stop by for a look. “He's been lying here, staring up at the sky, for more than 30 years.”

We're a few miles outside the town of Herning, although our own reasons for being here are more straightforward – we've come to witness a football match between local side Midtjylland and league leaders FC Copenhagen. At first glance, you'd be forgiven for thinking this is a complete mismatch.

From the capital, Copenhagen are Denmark's most successful club, with a record 16 league titles. Midtjylland, meanwhile, were only founded in 1999 following the merger of two second-tier rivals, and hail from a town with fewer than 60,000 inhabitants.

Yet the latter have rapidly grown into one of the country's most formidable sides, claiming four league titles in the past 12 seasons. Last term they won the Danish Cup, and beat both Celtic and Nottingham Forest in the Europa League. When we arrive, they trail only Copenhagen in the domestic league, heading into their table-topping clash. How have they managed it all?

We wave goodbye to Lenin and Birgitte in search of answers, driving through eerily quiet farmland outside Herning, to what appears to be a bunker from 007 adventure GoldenEye. Grey and austere, the building doesn't instantly strike you as welcoming – it turns out we couldn't be more wrong.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“We call this club the miracle from out of nowhere,” beams Midtjylland's bespectacled chairman Claus Steinlein, who shakes our hand enthusiastically before welcoming us into the warmth of the club's Dream 99 training complex. “Allow us to show you why.”

Opened in 2023, Dream 99 boasts a network of pristine football pitches, as well as a spa and gym. Steinlein leads us to a mural depicting the history of the club; a collage of black and white photos resembling newspaper cutouts. It's time for a history lesson.

“Midtjylland were formed from a merger between Herning Fremad and IFS,” he explains, pointing out a photo of the day the clubs came together – the suited, smiling chairmen shaking hands. “The name honours the Jutland province.” Indeed, Midtjylland means ‘Mid-Jutland' in Danish.

“We vowed from the start to become the biggest club in Denmark,” Steinlein adds. “People told us we were crazy. We knew that if we were to prove them wrong, we'd have to be different.”

Steinlein himself saw a way to help the new club stand out. “At that time, no Danish club had its own academy,” he says. “At least not with dedicated programmes. I wanted to be the first.”

Steinlein visited the academy of French side Nantes to learn what he could, returning with a blueprint for success. He asked the board to invest a massive chunk of its fledgling budget – around €800,000 – and, to his initial shock, they agreed. There was just one problem.

“Nobody wanted to send their kids here,” laughs Steinlein. “Children here grow up wanting to play for Brondby or Copenhagen, rather than Midtjylland. Convincing people was the first battle.”

A breakthrough came via Midtjylland's own kit man, who agreed to bring his 12-year-old son with him when taking the job. “It helped that his son was Simon Kjaer,” Steinlein says. “Simon went on to make more than 100 appearances for Denmark.”

Kjaer made a handful of first-team showings after graduating from the academy in 2007, before being sold to Palermo for €4m – a huge sum for a young Dane at the time. Steinlein's academy received a huge financial and reputational boost. “That gave our project the lift-off it needed,” he says.

Midtjylland began painstakingly forming partnerships across the region, more than 100 amateur sides regularly sending their best and brightest for trials. In exchange, Midtjylland provide equipment and tickets to first-team games. “It's about inspiring the next generation,” adds Steinlein.

Neither are Midtjylland's operations limited to the best Danish talent. We're led into an office to meet Jonas Dal, who heads the club's Nigerian academy.

“Every year, more than seven million children are born in Nigeria, compared with about 50,000 here, so the pool of talent is naturally much larger,” says Dal, who was once held at gunpoint during a visit to Lagos, but plays a key role in the Midtjylland project. “We bring over the most promising players. We have to be patient with them, because the weather and culture in Denmark are all very new to them.”

Right on cue, we meet Rilwan Hassan, who joined Midtjylland from the Lagos academy in 2010, before spending close to a decade playing for the club. He's now a coach with the academy. “It was so cold,” he recalls of his arrival as a teen. “But it was a massive opportunity. I was going into the unknown, but I quickly found out that this club was striving to be the very best. Everybody was pulling in the same direction.”

Many of Midtjylland's academy products, either from Nigeria or closer to home, are lured to the club with the promise they'll be sold if a bigger side comes in for them. Indeed, selling players has become a key aspect of Midtjylland's model. “If Liverpool or Barcelona come in for one of our players, that's perfect,” says Steinlein. “It means they've performed well and we can profit. Everybody wins.”

Following their formation, Midtjylland were immediately promoted to the top flight, before cementing themselves as consistent top-five finishers. Yet while results and youth development were impressive, they were beginning to struggle financially. Player sales barely covered the growing cost of operations, especially with European qualification hardly guaranteed each season.

“We'd wanted to become the biggest and best team in Denmark, but we were still some way off that,” winces Steinlein. “That soon changed, though.” The man who would help them take that next step was an Englishman with a physics degree, already making a name for himself at Brentford.

In June 2012, Matthew Benham had taken control of the Bees, then in League One, having made millions as the impresario of Smartodds – a company providing statistical analysis on sporting events to professional gamblers. That data also gave Benham extraordinary insight into how football games are won and lost, where and how goals are most often scored, and which players were being undervalued by the market. In short, a recipe for success.

That same year also saw Benham invite a Danish author to give a presentation to his staff. Benham had become fascinated by Rasmus Ankersen's book The Gold Mine Effect, which looked into cultural anomalies, such as why Jamaica consistently produces the best sprinters. Ankersen was equally impressed with Benham.

“At the time, Brentford were third in League One, and there were a couple of games to go,” the Dane would later recall. “I said to him, ‘What are the chances of you guys getting promoted?' When you ask that question, you expect an emotional yes or no, but he just said, ‘There's a 42.3 per cent chance.' That was when I knew he was a guy who was thinking very differently.”

Benham and Ankersen, the latter a promising player at Midtjylland before injury sent him down a different path, became firm friends. In 2014, the Dane convinced the data guru to invest in a second football club, with Benham paying £6.2m for a majority stake in Midtjylland. He brought with him his legion of statisticians, sports scientists and coaches. It was about to go turbo.

“This club now has tools to evaluate teams and players with much more accuracy using data,” said Ankersen, who was swiftly installed as chairman by Benham. “The model we're using could be applied in any country.”

Midtjylland's strategy was transformed overnight. “Set-pieces then became a fundamental part of the way we played,” Steinlein tells us on the balcony of the training complex, which overlooks the first-team's pitches. “They still are. We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes. The approach has been successful.”

In Benham's first year, Midtjylland were crowned Danish champions; their first major trophy. The team finished with a goal difference of plus 15 from set-pieces. “We were finally the best club in Denmark,” grins Steinlein. “A dream come true. Benham's stats and our focus on set-pieces were key.”

We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes

Next, Steinlein leads us into the main communal area of Dream 99. Above the only coffee machine in the building, where footfall is at its highest, a chart denoting Midtjylland's historical success from set-pieces adorns the wall. The 2015, 2018, 2020, 2024 and 2025 campaigns are highlighted as being particularly prolific – the Wolves won the league four out of five of those years.

“That one time we didn't win the title still bothers us,” laughs Steinlein. “We want our players and staff to be hurt by that, too. Topping this chart needs to be their motivation.”

Benham sold his stake in Midtjylland in 2023 to better focus on Brentford, though the two sides retain a close partnership. Today the club is owned by fashion tycoon Anders Holch Povlsen, Denmark's richest person, with an estimated worth of more than £12bn.

Ankersen has also departed, though his influence is still felt. A school called Guldminen, named after his book, was built into the Dream 99 complex. It aims to nurture both the best young sporting and academic talent in Denmark. FFT learns that students are given free rein of the building, meaning it isn't unusual for first-team players and schoolkids to share meals.

“We have a word for the environment we've fostered here: ‘sammenhold,'” says Steinlein. “It literally translates to ‘unity club', but it means so much more than that. It's about every person, from the kids to the first-teamers, coaches and cleaners, feeling part of something bigger. We are one entity. That's what sammenhold is, and it's our way of life.”

Overwhelmed by the scale and passion behind the Midtjylland project, FFT waves goodbye to the dream factory and makes our way over to the MCH Arena for tonight's crucial showdown against FC Copenhagen.

Inside the 12,000-capacity stadium, opened in 2004, FFT catch up with fans who are noisily drinking beer out of plastic cups and watching Brondby's early fixture on a big screen. Ahead of kick-off, we chat to lifelong Midtjylland fan Thomas Schouv Jacobsen. “My father is from Ikast, one of the two clubs that merged into Midtjylland,” he says. “Supporting this club since the start has been an extraordinary ride. The jump from winning a few silver medals to actually taking our first ever title in 2015 was indescribable. Seeing my father's face when we scored the decisive goal in the decisive match against Copenhagen is something that I'll never forget.”

Midtjylland's record against title rivals Copenhagen is certainly impressive.

Going into this game, the latter have won just twice in their past 14 meetings, with Midtjylland winning seven. Tonight, however, there's a fear that the league leaders might be too strong, especially given that regular Midtjylland defenders Rasmus Kristensen, Magnus Jensen and Martin Erlic are all out injured.

“We've had terrible setbacks in defence this season,” Jacobsen laments. “But, come May, we should have a very good chance of taking the championship. I think we have the best squad and the ability to come out successful.”

FFT also catches a moment with a Copenhagen fan. “We're massively important to Danish football because we have the biggest fanbase and play European football every year,” says lifelong supporter Kevin Willendrup.

“We're the flagship club. Our games against Brondby are by far the biggest in Denmark. There isn't the same level of hatred between the Midtjylland and Copenhagen fanbases – they've become extremely good in a very short space of time. Along with us, they're favourites to win the league every season. It's great that another team has emerged with so much quality.”

Yet there's no doubt in Willendrup's mind who'll emerge victorious tonight. “Copenhagen will win here for the first time in a long time,” he says. “We're on an incredible run under Bo Svensson and we're starting to look like a championship-winning team.”

As fans around us drain their beers and head inside, FFT does the same. We emerge onto the terraces to a magnificent sight. It's a record crowd, as flags swirl from the melee behind either end of the field. To our right, the home fans bellow into the evening sky and beat war drums. Off to our left, the white-clad Copenhagen fans are making their own thunderous racket.

Pitchside for the warm-ups, we see some familiar faces, including former Bournemouth beanpole Philip Billing, now at Midtjylland, and the ex-Cardiff targetman Andreas Cornelius, who is among the visitors' line-up. Curiously, Midtjylland's warm-up routine involves pain-staking set-piece practice; coaches repeatedly whipping vicious free-kicks into a packed box of giants.

As the players head inside to make their final preparations, we brush past former Everton and Real Madrid hard man Thomas Gravesen, who has presumably been loaned to a Danish TV outlet by the poker tables of Las Vegas. “Should be a good night tonight, guys,” he winks. “This is one of the biggest games of the season.”

The players emerge before kick-off to a deafening roar – the tifos, flags and rhythmic beating of drums providing an epic backdrop – before getting the game underway beneath the floodlights.

Copenhagen swiftly take charge but their dominance doesn't last. In the 12th minute, Midtjylland win a free-kick high on the left, not far from the corner flag. As Billing fizzes it in, FFT remarks that it's silly he isn't in the box himself given his size. He quickly shows us what we know, planting a ball squarely on to the head of onrushing Nigerian forward Friday Etim, whose effort crashes into the net to make it 1-0. Recorded wolf howls are played over the PA system as the roof comes off the MCH Arena.

Copenhagen dust themselves down and settle back into their rhythm, knocking the ball around menacingly, but they're unable to find a way through as Midtjylland's makeshift defence, marshalled by the imperious Andreas Maxso, clear everything.

Such low-block defending inevitably leads to mistakes, however, and one arrives just after the break, as wing-back Kjell Watjen fells Copenhagen skipper Thomas Delaney just inside the penalty area. The referee points to the spot and former Southampton star Mohamed Elyounoussi slots in an equaliser. The Copenhagen fans go wild.

The visitors take their possession up a notch. Robert Silva slaloms down the left and into the Midtjylland box, but his cutback is prodded away before the rebound is fired wide. Surely it's just a matter of time before they score again.

Then the unthinkable happens for the league leaders in the 62nd minute. Under very little pressure, Copenhagen goalkeeper Diant Ramaj passes straight to opponent Etim, who rounds the shot-stopper and shapes to pull the trigger, only to find his path blocked by recovering defenders.

As an entire stadium holds its breath, Etim squares the ball to Denil Castillo, arriving in support. The Ecuadorian fires low and hard into the Copenhagen net, and Midtjylland are in the lead once more, courtesy of a horrific error. Clearly shaken, Copenhagen never recover their rhythm. When the final whistle blows half an hour later, it's pure ecstasy for the Wolves supporters.

FFT rush onto the field to join the Midtjylland players as they celebrate in front of the frenzied home end. Arm in arm, players and coaches bounce in front of the melee, as we grab a word with Billing. “It's amazing when a result like this comes off,” he yells above the bedlam, with a huge smile on his face.

“We knew they'd play nice football, but that we could win it with our set plays and our physicality. We had to cope with a lot of injuries today, so the fact we came out of this game with a win is massive for us.”

When the players are finally separated from their adoring public, we're invited to join them inside. The dressing room is packed as victorious manager Mike Tullberg delivers a rousing speech in front of players, board members, staff and children. This must be what Steinlein meant by sammenhold. “I'm proud of you today, guys,” he says, singling out Maxso and his fellow defenders for an extraordinary performance. “There's a long way to go but we've given our ambitions a huge boost.”

A post shared by FourFourTwo (@fourfourtwouk)

Castillo, scorer of the winning goal, is also singled out in surprising fashion by the boss. “You've recently surpassed 100 games for us and what a way to cap it off,” Tullberg enthuses. “You keep playing like that and you won't be here for another 100.”

The whole room then erupts into an obscure song – a tradition that also sees players dancing and banging their lockers to the beat (watch the video above). It's a joyous scene. Afterwards, we head into chairman Steinlein's personal office, resembling a wood-panelled smoking room. The likes of Kenny Dalglish and Louis van Gaal have been guests here before us.

Drinks begin flowing and, at some point, FFT is only vaguely aware that the night is coming to an end. When we finally head back out into the cold Scandinavian air, it's with a sense that we've witnessed something truly spectacular – a wonder from nowhere.

With this result, there are just two points between Denmark's leading sides – one of them a traditional giant from an illustrious European city, the other a motley crew of dreamers and disrupters who refuse to accept the status quo.

It's the sort of revolution Vladimir Lenin, now lying flat on his back on a rain-soaked heath in our rear-view mirror, might have approved of.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

#1045. Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel said: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

“He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. What I saw, Jude was always the big brother that you imagine, taking care of his younger brother and making sure everything is alright. Behaving like a big brother. And that helps Jobe now. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”

The room is furnished in a typical Austrian style. Lots of wood, a fireplace, a few decorative touches. Through the large windows, you can see mountains surrounding the town of Saalfelden. Right on the dot, 21-year-old Jobe Bellingham arrives. It is August 2025, the midfielder has just signed for Borussia Dortmund and is giving his first press conference at the club’s training camp. German journalists are eager to find out what kind of character this talented youngster is. Will he provide any useful quotes for a story?

Half an hour later, the reporters are full of admiration and their notepads are full. Open-minded, self-assured, with clear opinions and a firm stance. That is how Bellingham presents himself. “It’s just not in my nature to be a superstar. I want to function like a machine,” he says. That was 15 months ago – a lot has happened since.

The fact he is progressing extremely well at Dortmund has been rewarded with this call-up from England manager Thomas Tuchel. A milestone for Bellingham, the next big step. At Dortmund he is playing an increasingly important role under manager Niko Kovac. To describe his style of play, you would most likely end up using his own expression: machine. Bellingham is becoming increasingly prominent and dynamic, his team-mates are looking to him more and more, and he is having a growing impact in attack. Ole Book, Dortmund’s sporting director, recently said: “He’s someone for the big stage.”
