"This England team are RUNNING RIOT in Spain" 🤩 👀 They lead the World Cup winners by 3-0 in Madrid!! WOW. https://t.co/2GuDnscRb4

It was only another Jarell Quansah error that got Spain back into the game. His mistake allowed Fermin López to play in Yamal for the run in which he was fouled by Anderson for the red card and the subsequent penalty.

Quansah is trying to do the hardest thing asked of a centre-half: play the ball out from the back. His red card in Mexico City and his mistake on Thursday against Croatia have not helped. Nevertheless, John Stones had a tricky start in an England shirt and developed into one of the team’s most important figures.

From another breakaway Yamal crossed for the substitute Williams to score Spain’s second. They would push again but England held on.

Thomas Tuchel praised England’s “statement win” that ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and secured top spot ahead of the world champions in the Nations League.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

“This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel said. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

“The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

He said: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

“The last half an hour felt like Azteca reloaded, to be honest. Again, it was a beautiful week. The commitment to get better is on the highest level.

“I said it many times, I love these players and I love the mentality .We’re building something and that was the next step. It was an amazing atmosphere. I will bottle it up for sure and then unfortunately we have to wait until the quarter-final.”

Asked what beating Spain can do for England’s belief, before the draw for the quarter-finals of the Nations League on Friday, Tuchel said: “You want confidence, not only through results, but confidence through performance and the result follows.

“That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got. We got it through the whole campaign of the Nations League, we trusted the process and improved our game and took steps forward match by match.

“We had a fantastic result and performance in Croatia followed up by a very good performance at home against Czechia. We then got our homework done against Croatia three days ago and that’s what we always wanted.

“We wanted to come back and compete on the highest level and see how far we can push our limits and how far we can push the opponent with the way we want to play and stay true to our identity. The team did excellent.”

England survived a Spanish fightback to round off their Nations League group-stage campaign in style with a 3-2 win over the world champions in Madrid.

Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored for the visitors with James Trafford pulling off a series of saves to prevent the hosts drawing level.

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

This is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

Asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel said: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

Speaking ahead of the match, Tuchel said: “I think we are ready to win. Now it’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength. I think that’s what we want to see. And then you can never predict the result in football, never. But it’s important that we show the mindset that you speak of and the spirit, and we will. I’m very confident about that.”

Meanwhile, fresh from lifting the World Cup in the summer, Spain have a 100% winning record in this season’s Nations League. They currently boast a staggering 43-match unbeaten run in all competitions, since losing a friendly to Colombia back in March 2024. England’s task is daunting, but not impossible.

#1002. The moment that galvanised England to deliver major statement against Spain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Three Lions shone at the Metropolitano, stunning the world champions with, as Miguel Delaney details, a key moment providing focus to their mission after World Cup heartache

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Spain vs England was a game that had almost everything, and may yet mean more; perhaps the most significant moment might have come before it had even started.

The hosts took the opportunity of a first match back in Madrid since the World Cup to showcase the trophy, in what almost felt another homecoming.

The mood was very much of revelling in their embossed status, something that would have had a particular edge for this specific nation.

No country that has won the World Cup has waited as long for another trophy as England.

And, as the 2010 winners Iker Casillas, Fernando Torres and Fernando Llorente presented Unai Simon that with that precious piece of brilliant gold, it was almost literally in England’s faces.

Thomas Tuchel’s side had to watch the goalkeeper wave the World Cup about right in front of them.

It had been noted on the Spanish side that Jude Bellingham was the only player who clapped, this now being the city that he calls home with Real Madrid. He then played like he was demanding the same appreciation, and he was not the only one.

As one figure with knowledge of the England camp said: “They will have been thinking ‘that’s what we want’.”

Seeing the World Cup so close and yet so far, with more than three years until the next edition, only deepened a mood that had been felt in the build-up to this game.

England, in the words of both Declan Rice and Thomas Tuchel, knew they were going to win.

“I could feel the true belief in the dressing room before the match that this is exactly the moment where we want to prove ourselves and push our limits,” the manager said.

They had that conviction to show what they were really about, and to show they would be the only team in the world not cowed by Spain. It was that mentality that comes when you feel ready to beat a rival that has long had it over you; that has been a benchmark.

A pace was set just moments after seeing that trophy, as a ferocious England subjected Simon to a flurry.

Just as importantly, they displayed a new level of their own, even beyond Tuchel describing it as the best performance of his time.

This wasn’t, after all, the usual counter-attacking approach to playing Spain - at least not for when England actually got so far ahead.

It was England imposing their game, an evolving ideology, on Spain.

“We are well aware which steps we took after the World Cup,” Tuchel said, conspicuously repeating this more than once.

The manager was deeply stung after all the criticism following the Argentina defeat.

And yet, much as he might bristle about it in public, it does feel as if some of that criticism has been acknowledged.

England look much more technical, but still with pace.

Throughout the World Cup, after all, there was a definite sense of his team just seeking to force their way through.

This was something much more considered and coherent.

“We wanted to get better in the deep build-up, we wanted to get better at defending in a low block and on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play on every opponent,” Tuchel remarked.

This similarly feeds into another theme of the night, which was how James Trafford’s performance may start a path that sees him become England’s No 1.

It was conspicuous that, when asked about the goalkeeper’s brilliant late double-save, Tuchel immediately pointed to his pure football effect.

“But there was a lot to do in the deep build-up as well, to overcome the first line of press, which he did very well with everyone around him,” he said. “So there was a lot to do, never lose the concentration, never lose the focus, never lose the vision, to find the free man to overcome the press and put the game into the opponent’s half.”

Tuchel clearly wants to change the very focus of this team.

And, in doing so, he wants to change its entire outlook.

There was naturally a lot of talk about “confidence” after a victory like this, which Tuchel was only too happy to immerse himself in.

“You want confidence, not only through results but confidence through performance and the result follows,” Tuchel said. “That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got.”

When Spain beat France in the World Cup semi-final with what was the performance of the tournament - “the statement performance” as Tuchel would have it - some close to Didier Deschamps’s squad felt the reason for the win had actually come much earlier.

Spain had beaten France in a series of high-profile games, above all the Euro 2024 and World Cup 2026 semi-finals. Lamine Yamal had been right to emphasise that, because he knew it played on French minds.

It gave Spain an edge. They knew they could beat France, but France were unsure if they could beat Spain.

That’s also why the frantic ending to this game in Madrid, so at odds with the first hour, may have been so important.

Had Spain equalised, or potentially won, England would have just been another team to fail to beat them. It could similarly have been the deepening of England’s own complex about Spain, since this would have been three high-profile set-backs in succession.

Even if this had just been a draw, after all, it would have felt like a defeat given it was a 3-0 lead.

It was a win, and a first defeat that Spain have endured in 44 games over two and a half years.

As such, England are not just another team the Spanish are reigning over.

They’re a team that know how to beat them, that can carry that through to a home Euros.

It might even create a bit of consideration on the Spanish side, even allowing for how assured they are in their own approach.

It might be the beginning of a proper modern rivalry.

Might, of course. England have to go and use this to do what Spain have made customary, and actually win one of those trophies.

Tottenham Hotspur have interest in Eli Junior Kroupi - but the move for a striker is shaping up for January

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tottenham Hotspur are to move for a new striker, as their search for goals intensifies.

The Lilywhites endured a terrible start to the season under manager Robert De Zerbi and were the last team in the Premier League to pick up a win – but after encouraging signs in recent weeks, it appears that they may have turned a corner.

With Tottenham struggling to score goals, however, a new forward has been earmarked for the January transfer window.

Spurs were said to be interested in Bournemouth forward Eli Junior Kroupi over the summer, but with the recent France international picking up a foot injury in preseason, any move to a bigger was put on hold.

De Zerbi instead brought in Omar Marmoush from Manchester City, with the Egyptian job-sharing the No.9 role with Dominic Solanke – though the pair have just two league goals between them this term.

With the North Londoners lacking a reliable hold-up man who can also offer threat in behind, attention has turned to Igor Matanovic of Freiburg.

Speaking on the Market Madness podcast, transfer expert Ben Jacobs claimed that the Croatian is an option for a loan move in January that Spurs could explore, with Bournemouth closing the door on Kroupi leaving midseason.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Cherries sold Semenyo to Manchester City in January – though the Ghanaian international only left when his release clause was triggered – and the south coast outfit are determined not to see another talent leave in the same way this campaign.

“If [Spurs] can’t find the right target, or maybe someone with a bit more experience within the Premier League, then they can reassess in the summer,” Jacobs claimed.

“What they won’t want to do is necessarily go all in and panic buy in January for someone on a long-term contract, instead of just biding their time and waiting it out.”

Tottenham spent around £400 million in the summer building a side that finished 17th two years running, smashing their transfer record twice and recruiting seven new faces.

Every one of De Zerbi's signings over the summer – including youngsters such as Cole Ramsey and backup goalkeeper Martin Dubravka – was signed from an English side.

Matanovic is worth €30m, according to Transfermarkt. Tottenham take on Ipswich Town when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#999. Jorge Jesus responds to criticism from Cristiano Ronaldo’s mum as Portugal retirement row rumbles on

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international football earlier this month

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus has defended himself in the wake of remarks from Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother as the dispute over the forward’s international retirement continued in Wales.

Ronaldo called time on his Portugal career on 5 November, less than a month after the Portuguese Football Federation handed him a 30-day suspension and a fine of 255 euros (approximately £210) for walking out on the national team.

The 41-year-old had left the squad last month shortly before a Nations League fixture in Denmark following a row with Jesus after he was an unused substitute in Portugal’s win over Norway.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward’s mother, Dolores Aveiro, said she was pleased by the result as Denmark crushed Portugal 4-1 in the Braga return on Saturday, because her son had been deceived by Jesus.

“Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus said at his pre-match press conference in Cardiff.

“She is a lady I greatly respect, she suffered a lot to raise her children.”

Asked if debate about Ronaldo’s retirement from international football would stop, Jesus said: “I don’t know when it’s going to stop. If you guys (reporters) ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.”

Portugal will be without the suspended pair of Joao Palhina and Ruben Dias in Cardiff, with Manchester United playmaker Bruno Fernandes set to take over the captaincy in the absence of the injured Bernardo Silva.

Barcelona defender Joao Cancelo returns after missing the Denmark game through suspension.

Jesus said: “I am going to change some players, but it’s not only physical. We have four players on yellow cards. After the game against Denmark everyone is asking me about different individuals, not about the team or winning here.

“If we win we will have 15 points, which is only matched by England and Spain. We played one bad game and it’s harder to move on when we have a result like that, but we are going to try and win the game.”

Heading into Tuesday’s game, Portugal are three points clear of Denmark as they aim to secure top spot in their Nations League group.

#998. Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Download the Nature Podcast 13 November 2026

The past year has been... a lot. Record-breaking temperatures, devastating floods and catastrophic wildfires have brought the realities of climate change into sharp focus for people around the world. At the same time, many governments and organisations have scaled back on their climate action.

If you’re anything like me you might be feeling it’s all a bit ‘doom and gloom’. So in this series I decided to face my climate anxiety head on and set out in search of reasons for optimism.

In this first episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about what the data really show and why there are still reasons to hope.

00:00 How climate change feels overwhelming

21:49 How are the world’s nations doing on climate change?

Nature: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target

Nature: How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

Nature: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

This episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Daniel Knowler, Akio Jefferson, Lionel Cohen and The Conductor, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Hannah Ritchie, Ketan Joshi and Niklas Höhne for featuring in this episode.

I’m going to be honest with you. I worry a lot.

I worry about all sorts of things. Money, friends, family, if my voice is weird as you’re listening to it... but there’s one thing I’ve been worried about since I was a teenager in the early 2000s. The climate.

Those anxieties have only gotten worse. In recent years, it has felt like climate action has stalled. In 2024, the world passed the 1.5˚C ‘threshold’ set in Paris for the first time. Shortly thereafter, Donald Trump returned to the White House and on the first day of his Presidency set about reversing climate policies of the previous administration, vowing to promote fossil fuels. In Europe, right-wing politicians have taken aim at climate goals, with the EU weakening previously ambitious environmental policy. All while it’s getting hotter and hotter. In May there were record breaking temperatures in my home of the UK , then in June those records were broken again, twice in the same week in fact, with temperatures in some places across the continent more than ten degrees hotter than they were between 1991-2020. That was the story all over Europe. Without climate change, it’s extremely unlikely Europeans would have had to endure these heatwaves. And globally, scientists of all stripes have expressed doubts that any government has done enough to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.

So, it feels like we’re failing on climate, heck, I can even look outside my window and see evidence for that. But what’s weird is that even as climate change is affecting me more, I find it harder to engage with.

As things get worse, I’m having trouble staying optimistic that we, you me and everyone, can do anything about it. And that’s an odd position to be in, as a science journalist. Climate change is one of the biggest stories of our time.

Every week, we pick out stories to cover on the podcast. And I always want to report the latest climate science, and I do, but I find it hard. Sometimes it just feels like more bad news at a time when our audience, and I, could do with less. I feel hopeless.

But is that actually right? Am I justified in that feeling? As the one thing I know about science is often the truth is a bit more complicated than we think. So, while the narrative can feel overwhelming negative, is that really what the data says?

To try and shake myself out of this climate funk, talking to some of the scientists and campaigners on the front lines of climate research, and what I found was a story of: Tipping points…

That has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge.

I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions.

The system is changing at exponential speed.

This is Cooked? a three-part miniseries for Nature, where I try and find out whether we are well… cooked. Is it game over for climate or are there reasons for hope? I’m your host Nick Petrić Howe. And in this first episode, I decided to start with the data, and I had a good idea of who might be able to help me with that.

As a data scientist, I'm biased. And I would say, look at the data to understand for these big problems, where they're coming from, why they're happening, and importantly, what we can do to solve them.

In the past year or so, I’ve found myself struggling with anxiety about the climate. But a couple of years ago a book came out that seemed to fly against what I had assumed was the case, as it stated, backed up with oodles of data, that it isn’t the end of the world. So, I knew I wanted to speak to its author — Hannah Ritchie.

What I wanted to do in that book was, think, twofold.

That’s Hannah, the author of ‘Not the end of the world’ and a data scientist at our World in Data and the University of Oxford.

One was that I was trying to write it to my former self, who was very, very pessimistic, wasn't sure if there was really a future there for me and present where we are now. And the point is not that these problems are solved in any way, they're still huge problems, but we have started to make progress and there's lots of opportunity for us to make more progress. My point is not that we should be complacent and optimistic that these problems will solve themselves. I think it's to kind of maybe get rid of a bit of the cynicism that there's nothing that we can do and actually no one is doing anything because I don't think that's true. And I think the second kind of motivation for doing that is to look at the data and understand if we want to solve these problems, what are the really key and big things that we need to do to solve them?

The book looked at seven huge challenges that humanity faces, including climate change, examining each through the lens of data, to understand the progress we have and haven’t made on them, and what we should do. So I was curious to hear from Hannah about how we were actually doing on climate change.

If you go back 10 years, the world we were sitting in when the world signed the Paris Agreement was that the alternatives to fossil fuels were much more expensive than fossil fuels. For solar and wind were way more expensive. Batteries were extremely expensive. Electric vehicles were basically not on the radar at that point. So it seemed very, very hard to me at the time to see how the world would actually progress on this. What we've seen over the last decade is this huge drop in the costs of these low-carbon energy sources. And that now means that they're cost competitive with fossil fuels, right? So you have the kind of short-term incentive of picking the low-cost solution, now adding up and aligning with the long-term issue we're trying to solve, which is climate change.

These days renewable energy is very cheap. Let’s take solar energy as an example. Between 2009 and 2025, estimates from the investment firm Lazard suggest solar energy prices have dropped to less than a sixth of what it used to cost on average. This number even includes the continued costs of running solar plants, making them, along with wind, the cheapest form of energy.

This change has helped Hannah go from pessimistic to optimistic about the future of climate change. It’s not just that the costs have tumbled, more and more this ‘clean’ energy is actually being implemented as well.

We now also see that many countries are now rolling out clean energy at an increasingly fast pace. So it's not like it's just that the cost has dropped. You can actually now start to see that translating into action.

Hannah also thinks that this electrification of the world has other benefits too.

What's really key about that electrification lever, and I think is under appreciated, is how much you gain there in terms of efficiency. You know, it's not just we want to do this because it saves us carbon emissions, which it will if we were powering that through low carbon power, but also you get huge efficiency gains from this. like driving in an electric car uses about a third of the energy of driving in a petrol car, right? So you actually also get rid of lots of this energy waste that we currently have in the system.

Worldwide, adoption rates of electric vehicles are increasing. Around a quarter of every new vehicle sold is electric, and in some countries this rate is much higher. In Norway 97% of new cars sold were electric, while in China 53% were. Now, many people are critical of electrical vehicles for various reasons. Mining of lithium for use in batteries can be very environmentally damaging, for instance. And using public transport is better than having a personal electric vehicle most of the time. But when it comes to their climate credentials, electric cars beat conventional every time.

The world has also been built in many places to favour vehicles and in some areas public transport is not a viable option. So if we want the most people to use the least climate emission causing form of transport, electric vehicles will be part of the mix.

But it’s not just data on clean energy and electrification that gives Hannah hope. She also points to progress that’s been made in making steel and concrete production more climate conscious. They’re maybe a bit less obvious in our day to day lives, as most of us don’t work on big construction projects, but these core components of buildings come with big emissions. Cement production, for example, accounted for around 6% of global carbon emissions as of 2024 according to the International Energy Agency.

But this is down from a peak in 2021, due to slowed growth in construction, and is projected to decrease further as improvements are made to the recipe for cement, or alternatives to it entirely are created.

These solutions haven't been scaled yet. They're at a very, very small level, but I think we still have made progress there and there are actually solutions starting to come online and starting to get cost competitive, but it will take some time for them to build up to a kind of level where you would actually start to see dents in the data.

As Hannah said, the point of her book and this examination of the data is not to allow us all to pat ourselves on the back and say ‘job’s a good ‘un’. There’s still a lot that we need to do, and in many ways some of these changes aren’t happening fast enough. Rather the point is to not make us feel despondent and hopeless, as that helps nobody.

And there are actually reasons for optimism. Falling prices in renewables, increased electrification and more climate-conscious construction are all starting to make dents in the data according to Hannah.

So maybe I don't need to be so worried after all. assuming of course that we can keep this up.

Renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is making the rise in emissions less bad.

There's a new disruptive and energy-intensive technology out there that could stall climate progress. Artificial intelligence.

The level of debate about this technology is massive. It's actually really fascinating because I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

Whenever I open social media these days, I see a lot of scepticism about artificial intelligence. I don’t have to scroll far to come across a video of someone pretending to be a large language model powered chatbot who says silly things while chugging litres of water. But the backlash against the technology is spilling out of social media and pouring into real world legislation. We've seen the first moratoriums on the building of data centres, the facilities that house the infrastructure for AI and other internet services. And often the cited reasons are environmental — water and electricity use.

So that got me wondering, if AI is so energy intensive could it stall climate progress? Especially as many of these data centres are using fossil fuels to meet their energy needs. For the sake of this podcast, I’m just going to focus on energy demands, as that’s what’s more relevant to the climate, and put other environmental concerns to one side for now.

To do so, I wanted to put those memes aside as well and find out what the data actually says. So, I reached out to an expert on data centres and their energy use to go through some of the numbers.

My name is Ketan Joshi. I'm an independent researcher and analyst, working on energy and data centres and fossil fuel phase-out.

Ketan has been working as energy analyst for many years, but more recently has been focusing on how much energy data centres consume, particularly for artificial intelligence. I wanted to know how a growth in data centres would affect the climate, but he explained to me that that’s a quite a difficult thing to work out.

We have thousands of projections of data center growth into the near future. But the level of variation that you see in these projections makes me almost want to never use them. and the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway, you know, it'll grow to maybe four to five percent by twenty thirty. I've seen ones that are up to like twenty percent of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway. You know, it'll grow to maybe 4 to 5% by 2030. I've seen ones that are up to like 20% of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind this wild skew of future projections is because there is an inherent assumption about the future of artificial intelligence and the shape and form that it takes in the near future. The way that we tend to formulate projections just falls apart with something like this where there is an inherent uncertainty as to what the technology is, what it's going to be used for, whether it's hype, whether it's real, whether we go for high energy consumption models or low energy consumption models. There's like 10 crisscrossing vectors of uncertainty that make it really, really hard to say what's going to happen.

The future is, unfortunately, unpredictable. It’s hard to know what AI will look like in 10 years, or even 10 days for that matter. So, it’s tough to fit into our projections of the future and how it may impact the climate. As a result, Ketan likes to focus on the here and now to see what we can understand about the technology. To start, it’s important to note that while AI gets a lot of attention, it currently forms a small part of energy usage. The International Energy Agency, for instance, estimates that data centres use — for everything, not just AI — around 2% of the world’s energy. As Ketan says, that may grow — perhaps by a lot, perhaps by not so much. It’s part of the uncertainty with the technology.

According to Ketan’s analyses, though, AI and by that, I mean the generative kind that powers chatbots, may be particularly energy intensive.

Something that I've found in the past few weeks actually, having looked at some of the new newer corporate statements. So for instance, Microsoft analyzed their latest statement, I analyzed Google and Amazon. And all three of those companies are using more energy to earn the same amount of revenue, if that makes sense.

Rather than working towards more efficiency as computing has done in the past, Ketan thinks that companies are using more and more energy to try and make cleverer chatbots, or autonomous AI agents. Google and Microsoft for example, have acknowledged that they’ve increased their energy usage as they build out AI capacity.

One thing to note here is that different use cases of AI have different energy demands. Techniques like Machine Learning which often gets labelled AI, don't use as much energy as generative AI like Large Language Models. And then within generative AI, things like a written response from a chatbot needs a lot less energy than generating an image or a video.

But the concern for the climate is that all this energy needs to come from somewhere. And if there isn’t sufficient renewable energy in place, it will come from fossil fuels.

Figuring out how much data centres may be using fossil fuels, though, is not easy. Ketan explained to me that when companies report their power consumption it’s not quite as simple as them just stating what proportion of renewable energy versus fossil fuels they’ve used. Similarly to carbon offsets, companies can purchase certificates from renewable energy providers and then use them to show that their emissions are lower than they are. Microsoft recently stopped using this method, which has been widely criticised, and in their most recent report there was a large rise in their emissions.

The companies can also have positive effects on renewable energy. With their vast resources they can fund new wind and solar farms. Microsoft, for example, has announced a $6 billion agreement to build AI infrastructure powered by renewables in Norway. Deals such as these can also then be included in companies’ reports on what kinds of energy they use.

So, untangling all of this is pretty tricky. With that in mind, Ketan explained how energy use has changed in the US, where there’s the most data centres in the world.

There's a new report from the energy information administration, updating on 2025 data. And of course, you know, emissions have gone up. They haven't gone up crazy. Like they haven't gone, you know, it's not like it’s skyrocketing, you know, right angle, but they have gone up and renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is just making the rise in emissions less bad.

The report Ketan mentioned says that US energy-related CO2 emissions went up by about 2% in 2025. That may not sound like a lot, but it’s against a backdrop of emissions falling, so any rise is a cause for concern for the climate. And like Ketan says, renewable energy adoption has continued apace, so the fact that there were more renewables, but emissions still went up implies that more energy was coming from carbon-emitting fossil fuels.

This is backed up by a report from the Energy Institute, a UK-based professional body that monitors energy use. The report said that US emissions had increased in 2025 due to higher coal use, and that electricity demand had risen faster than supply driven in part by data centres and artificial intelligence. An independent research firm, the Rhodium group, also identified a rise in carbon emissions in the US and cited a particularly cool winter, more coal use and increased demand in electricity from data centres as reasons.

Of course, data centres could be powered by renewable energy, but building this supply takes time and if we have a sudden increase in energy demand, due to AI for instance, then fossil fuels could be used to plug the gap. Google, for example, has acknowledged that it’s expanding its AI development on a grid that is undersupplied with clean energy, but still remains a large funder of clean energy projects. Google still plans to reduce their emissions, but right now, they’re using more fossil fuel energy.

Ketan would like to see more transparency from the tech companies creating AI on its environmental impacts, so it can be scrutinised more easily, along with more regulation from governments. He also thinks that everyone has a role to play deciding on what terms we use this technology.

Ketan is actually optimistic about the future, as it seems that the general public are beginning to understand that they do have the power to demand better from these companies. Environmental, cost and climate concerns are being raised against AI, and politicians are listening — you can look to the growth of moratoriums on data centres to see that. To be clear this isn’t just because of climate, opponents of data centres describe them as being ugly, straining local resources and not providing many tangible benefits to their residents. These are issues that affect people no matter what side of the political divide they sit on. And this bipartisan opposition has meant that politicians have started taking action.

But that touches on another thing I wondered about. What are governments and nations actually doing? Are they meeting the goals they’ve set out for climate? And it’s certainly felt to me like there’s been some backsliding recently — with right-wing politicians taking aim at climate goals.

So, what does the data say about how the nations of the world are doing?

Well, it's better than we used to think 10 years ago, but it's definitely not there where it should be.

If you’ve ever engaged with climate change, you’ll know that it’s a global issue. The whole world is getting hotter and that affects all of us. Because of that, nations often get together and come up with various pledges on what they’re going to do about that. What comes out of these pledges is ultimately what we, as a global society, are doing about climate change.

And I knew a scientist who keeps close tabs on this, so I gave him a call.

Hello. Niklas Höhne, New Climate Institute, calling in from Cologne, Germany.

I met Niklas a few years ago at COP26, the enormous climate conference run by the UN. He co-founded the New Climate Institute, a non-profit that works on climate policy, where he oversees analyses on climate policy. I was there reporting for Nature and I asked him, even back then, if things were hopeless. I remember that he didn’t coddle me or make me despair. He gave a nuanced picture. So, I caught up with him to see where we are now.

So while 10 years ago we thought global greenhouse gas emissions would rise forever and would lead to a temperature increase of three and half degrees by the end of the century, we now think that with currently implemented policies, they will stabilize and decline and then lead to around two and a half degrees by the end of the century. So a full degree better than we thought only 10 years ago. So that's remarkable. That's really good. But it's not enough. The Paris agreement says well below two or in the direction of 1.5 and there we are far away from it. And also, we have to say that in the past years, global greenhouse gas emissions have still increased. So despite all of the efforts, is still more fossil fuels being burned each year and therefore we have more greenhouse gas emissions each year and that means not only are we not stopping climate change, we are fuelling climate change. So, we are accelerating the speed of change each year by adding more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere than we had in the year before.

The main driver of this drop in the projected temperature increase

is something that Hannah already touched on — the speed of renewable energy production.

Prices are falling and Niklas thinks this may push us to precipice to start some exponential change.

Niklas Höhne: I think the last 10 years we've been surprised each year about the speed of renewable energy, electrification and the transformation that has been started. So, I assume that also next year and the years after we will be positively surprised because the end of that development of the technologies is not there. Yeah. So, prices still decline. New battery technologies are invented. Renewables are incredibly cheap compared to 10 years and are still declining. And what we as humans often underestimate is exponential change. The system is changing at exponential speed. And that means each year more solar is implemented than we thought before or more batteries are implemented, more electric cars. And most of the models, they are still kind of assuming a linear change and underestimate the speed of the transformation. And that's why I think I'm quite optimistic about our future projections that this renewable energy transformation will actually win against the fossil fuels because it's simply exponential change. And that always has to win over a linear trend, which is the one described by the fossil fuels.

You can see a similar exponential change if you look at the history of cars.

At the turn of the twentieth century there was blight on cities — horses. According to the London Transport museum in 1900 there were 300,000 horses in London. But just 14 years later they’d all but disappeared. This sudden departure of the city’s workhorses helped humanity solve a pretty relevant problem for a climate podcast — pollution

Horses produced a lot of… waste — you know the kind of waste I'm talking about — that was very literally clogging up streets. The solution, ironically, given the topic of the podcast, was cars. Motorized vehicles had actually been around for a few years in the early 20th Century, but it wasn’t really until 1908 when the Model-T ford came out, the first car affordable to a large number of people, that they really took off. In 1910 there were 8000 cars registered in London, in 1920 there were 190,000, the next year there were 250 000 And as cars took off, streets once clogged with horse manure instead became roads for motorcars.

That may seem like a pretty inevitable change, but if you were a Londoner in 1900, you’d probably wouldn’t have believed that the world could be so different in a few decades.

Perhaps renewable energy will be the same for us. It may seem like we’ll never overcome our addiction to fossil fuels, but as prices tumble, maybe we’re standing on the cliff edge of that exponential change.

So there are certainly positives for the climate. The speed of the energy transition has taken many experts by surprise. But beyond that, there’s still a long to go. And when it comes to how countries are actually sticking to their climate pledges, it was a bit of a mixed bag.

We regularly look at who is basically the best, which is the best country around the world. And the places one, two, three are always empty. So, no country is doing everything correct. But in each area, you can see quite positive things. We have electric mobility, which is shooting off and was shooting off in Norway because Norway supported it significantly with a lot of money. But now it's basically the better way of doing things. So even countries like Vietnam or Nepal have very high adoption rates for electric cars. They sell more electric cars than conventional vehicles in these countries. And that is remarkable because it shows that this is the most economic way of having individual mobility. Then there's other areas, buildings and industry, which really are a bit behind. And it's very difficult to find really good examples where countries are really doing well. But OK, I think also in buildings and in industry, this idea of electrification is something that will now take off as well. So in buildings, it's heat pumps for heating, which are the new normal. So, there's huge opportunity to do more in those areas as well.

You may have noticed that some of the biggest emitters haven’t been mentioned there. And to be honest, they were some of the ones I was most worried about. China and the US.

China is the world’s top emitter according to the International Energy Agency, but it seems that their emissions are finally starting to peak — meaning that the greenhouse gases they emit may be starting to reduce. According to some analyses, they have already peaked. This is likely because they have implemented a huge amount of renewable energy. Last year, China installed more solar capacity than the rest of the world combined, although this boom in installation is slowing down a bit now.

And as Niklas explained to me, China has also been instrumental in producing what the world needs for renewable energy — they’re the leading manufacturer of solar, wind and battery technology. But he did impress on me that that wouldn’t have been possible without the policies of several countries, especially in Europe, promoting renewables and therefore creating the right market conditions for China.

And then there’s world’s second biggest emitter and the largest historical contributor to climate change. The US. There I was worried about the influence of the most recent administration. Trump’s Team has dealt a severe blow to the world’s ability to tackle climate change, by walking away from Paris Agreement on Climate, for the second time. They also repealed the ‘endangerment finding’ that set out that climate change is a public threat and has been used to enact climate policy. And they have spent billions trying to undo climate projects, giving the companies behind them refunds if they instead invest that money in fossil fuels. These actions, the administration say, would save the United States money by removing excess regulations, lower bills for families and help maintain the US’s leadership. But they are counter to what climate scientists say we should be doing — we need to stop burning fossil fuels and rein in our emissions.

So, I was expecting a pretty negative response from Niklas when I asked about how the US is doing. But he had a few surprises for me.

So for the US as such, it's the second largest emitter and the Trump administration has basically dismantled all climate policies that were there from the federal government in the US. And that means now that the emissions in the US will still continue to decline, but will decline slower.

This first surprise, is that while the actions of the Trump administration will likely increase the emissions that the US will produce, that is against a backdrop of overall decline. Even though there's been a recent uptick in emissions in the past year, the US's emissions have been steadily falling since the early 2000s and that will likely continue. Albeit not as fast as it would if the Trump administration was more pro climate. Ultimately, the economics of clean energy are hard even for the most powerful country in the world to fight against — it’s getting harder and harder to justify the use of fossil fuels when the alternatives are cheaper.

The second surprise was an unexpected way that the current US administration may have unintentionally pushed for a move away from fossil fuels.

Which is the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. And that created a significant energy crisis with very, very high fossil fuel prices for oil and gas. And that created a push towards energy efficiency and renewable energy. And that effect will be significant. It's very difficult to quantify that right now. But from our point of view, it's very clearly that that will has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge, so to say, and over the tipping point that it will be self-propelling because all the countries that currently suffer significantly from fuel shortage is not even a price, a high price is really a shortage that simply have not enough. They will now really, really think about alternatives and have already. So, some countries have already increased their renewable energy targets. China has reduced their oil consumption by 10 to 20%, depending on which source you look at within only 12 months. So, there's significant changes on the way that will reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

As Niklas mentioned, data on this is hard to get, and this is still an evolving story. Time will tell what the impacts of the war in Iran may be. There have in fact been moves towards and away from renewable energy as a result of surging oil and gas prices — with nations like India and South Korea burning more coal in response to the higher gas prices, while people in the Philippines have taken to installing rooftop solar panels at record rates to avoid the high oil prices. So, a true accounting of the effect of the closure of the strait of Hormuz will take some time. But Niklas’s assessment is backed up by an increased sale of electric vehicles and a record high in solar exports from China, and an analysis by Carbon Brief that suggests that global emissions may fall in 2026. This has led some to wonder whether the war in Iran will be a tipping point for energy — that it will finally end humanity’s addiction to fossil fuels.

Overall, while there are clearly some areas in which the world is behind on its targets, it’s perhaps not as dire as I thought. In terms of renewable energy, adoption is accelerating. True, the current pace won’t be enough to meet our climate goals. We need to stop emitting carbon altogether, and soon if we're to meet the 1.5° target set in Paris, and even then we'll probably have to take some carbon out of the atmosphere. But Niklas, even with all the caveats, was optimistic about the future.

We have all the tools at hand and even now it's economic and the obstacle is not technology, the obstacle is not cost. The obstacle is our inertia in the system and that some lose something and some others gain something. And that is something we as a society really have to overcome.

So, while there’s still a long way to go, there are reasons for optimism. Renewable energy has outperformed many researchers expectations, and continues to do so, in spite of the backlash against it in some quarters. Which, I’ll be honest, does make me feel better. The data tell me that it’s not completely hopeless. When cities were overwhelmed by horses and their waste, cheap motor vehicles changed things in a matter of decades. I’m hopeful that renewable energy can do the same here.

But this is what the data says, largely about what we’ve already done. I was also curious about what we should do in the future. What are some of the big ideas that can help tackle climate change? That’s next time.

We could sit here and say well people should just do this because they should just care about the climate and reducing their emissions. But I think having very good affordable substitutes for people to switch to is just really, really crucial.”

Liverpool will not look to the transfer market to replace Virgil van Dijk in January - or next summer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool are accused of having an unbalanced squad this season, however, the club will reportedly resist the urge to recruit a new centre-back during the January transfer window.

The Athletic claim that adding to the heart of the defence is 'not a priority' for the Reds, ruling out investment in the position for both the upcoming winter market and the summer of 2027.

Instead of turning to the transfer market to silence critics, the Liverpool hierarchy is placing its trust in the crop of emerging defensive talent to eventually succeed 35-year-old Virgil van Dijk.

Liverpool's decision is largely down to the impact Jeremy Jacquet has had since arriving at Anfield. Behind him, Anfield still has high hopes for a trio of highly-rated youngsters: Giovanni Leoni, who is nearing a return to fitness following an ACL injury last year, Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who is currently on loan with Levante in Spain, and teenage prospect Mor Talla Ndiaye.

Opposition supporters and media pundits have spent much of the season pointing out a lopsided squad that is forcing Iraola into tactical compromises on a weekly basis, as well as Van Dijk's advancing years.

The primary target of this criticism is the club’s full-back situation with Conor Bradley sidelined and Jeremie Frimpong unfancied in a traditional back-four system.

Iraola has been forced to deploy centre-backs, most notably Ronald Araujo, as makeshift right-backs. And while the Uruguayan has brought physical solidity and aggression, asking a traditional central defender to provide the overlapping width hasn't always had the desired effect and on occasion left Liverpool looking somewhat asymmetrical in possession.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Square pegs in round holes is never a sustainable fix, and coupled with a lack of midfield depth, squad planning is never far from the Anfield conversation.

If Liverpool are officially ruling out central defensive reinforcements, even with Virgil van Dijk entering the twilight of his career, funds and focus can theoretically be redirected toward the squad’s weaknesses.

In FourFourTwo's opinion, their January priority must be identifying a specialist right-back and a dominant midfield presence, although Trey Nyoni's emergence as a water-carrier of sorts makes up for that to an extent. The lasting message from the corridors of power at Anfield is that in the centre of defence, Liverpool consider themselves already locked down for the foreseeable future.

#996. How Andy Robertson defied the odds to become Scotland’s greatest captain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

A humble Robertson insists he is not on the level of Sir Kenny Dalglish, despite overtaking the legendary forward on 103 caps, but Jamie Braidwood outlines how the captain carved out a unique legacy through work-ethic and commitment

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It was a burst from the left wing that would be seen time and time again. Andy Robertson’s first goal for Scotland came on just his fourth appearance for his country, at 20 years old and only a few months after completing a £2.85m move from Dundee United to Hull City. The wider importance of the goal was ultimately forgotten, a late consolation against England in a 3-1 defeat at Celtic Park. But for Robertson, with his wide-eyed excitement and the determination to carry his run forward, it was the moment that set the tone for what was to follow.

Twelve years later, Robertson has overtaken the great Sir Kenny Dalglish to become the most-capped Scotland’s men’s player of all time, passing his hero and legend for both his childhood club, Celtic, and adopted one, Liverpool, with his 103rd international appearance against Switzerland. It is only in keeping with Robertson’s humility that he was the first to insist Dalglish remains Scotland’s greatest player; it is only in keeping with Dalglish’s typical wry humour that he reminds Robertson that his own tally of international appearances would be much higher had competitions like the Nations League been around in his day.

“It’s not really about me,” Robertson said ahead of taking the record. "It’s about him [Dalglish] in my opinion. For how long the record stood, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is.”

But Scotland will celebrate Robertson, too. What is not up for debate is the scale of achievement and the remarkable nature of his journey. His story is well known yet will be retold many times this week: how a boy released by Celtic for being too small and who worked in the Hampden ticket office while playing part-time with Queen’s Park would become one of the world’s best left-backs and a Champions League and Premier League winner.

With Scotland, part of Robertson’s legacy is formed by qualifying for three major tournaments in five years, when the Tartan Army had not previously been on the big stage since 1998. Robertson was the leader on each campaign under Steve Clarke, from the penalties against Serbia to reach Euro 2020 to beating Spain and Norway to deservedly make Euro 2024. Then, in the delirium that was Scotland’s win over Denmark to qualify for the World Cup, it was Robertson who provided another moment of inspiration when he poignantly remembered his late friend Diogo Jota and the promise they had made to each other while watching the 2022 World Cup four years before.

Robertson has led his nation with dignity and class and if insists that Dalglish remains the King, the counter is to suggest that he stands, by some way, as Scotland’s greatest captain. He has worn the armband 80 times, with an 81st cap as skipper to come in St Gallen, putting him well clear of George Young, on 48, and Billie Bremner, on 39. Robertson took on the armband just four years after his senior debut, at the age of 24. Should he continue through to Euro 2028 and Scotland, as co-hosts, ensure their place, he may lead the Tartan Army at a fourth major tournament and mark a 10-year stint as captain. The history of the Scotland men’s national team is around 150 years old, yet he would hold another record.

Euro 2028 could be important in another respect. For although Scotland have enjoyed a golden period in terms of qualifying for major tournaments, they have underperformed in all of them and have yet to escape the group stage. The missing piece for this generation of players, which they could hold above those of the past, remains out of reach. For Robertson, he will not need reminding that Clarke’s considerable achievements as head coach come with the reality that Scotland failed to perform on the big stage, with the 1-0 win over Haiti in Boston in June their only victory in nine attempts at major tournaments. Now under a fourth head coach with Scotland, in Sebastien Pocognoli, there is still time to amend that, with a chance to still secure promotion to League A, should they beat the Swiss and receive a favour from North Macedonia.

It has not helped Robertson that during his time as Scotland captain two of the other home nations have been led by talismanic captains in Harry Kane and Gareth Bale, players who brought attacking inspiration and who could change a game in the flick of a switch. Robertson’s rise and formidable peak at Liverpool came when he was part of a machine, where the driving runs of the flying left-back fitted in with the movement of the front three and the organisation of the midfield. At Scotland, Robertson has provided plenty of assists and thrust, but, unlike his old team-mate Trent Alexander-Arnold, he is not the sort to orchestrate from full-back.

Robertson has, however, worked to squeeze everything he could possibly get from his career. Perhaps it was overcoming rejection that made him take nothing for granted, but Robertson has made history by turning the ordinary into extraordinary: by showing up camp after camp, for never letting his country down. There is the work-ethic, the commitment, the desire to push for every cap as if it is his last. There are the personal touches, too, forming a spirit and a togetherness that took a Scotland squad further than they had done in a generation. But above all, Robertson continued to play the game in the way he always vowed to: as if he was a fan who had just come down from the stands. And in his relentless pursuit, he has made a nation proud along the way.

#995. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

Gareth Bale is involved in an investment project to buy Sevilla.

The former Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid man retired from playing football three years ago after a stint in Major League Soccer with Los Angeles Galaxy, at the age of 34.

Since retiring, Bale has been occasionally involved in punditry and competed in the February 2023 edition of the AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am golf tournament in California – but now, he appears to be heading down the same route as the likes of Ronaldo and Gerard Pique in owning a Spanish club.

Seven-time Europa League winners Sevilla have fallen on hard times since winning the competition for the last time in 2023, failing to finish in the top half of La Liga for the past four seasons and narrowly scraping relegation in 2025, while city rivals Real Betis go from strength to strength.

Bale played against the Andalusian outfit nine times in his career, registering nine goals and assists – and after leaving Madrid with a fractured relationship between him and fans, he might be about to create more distance by investing at the Estadio Ramon Sanchez Pizjuan.

El Confidecial in Spain are reporting that the Welsh wing wizard is linked to an ownership group looking to take over the club.

American investment fund Juggernaut Capital Partners are one of three groups said to be interested in the club, along with rival group HD Ventures, led by Saudi brothers Mansour Sayed and Haidar Sayed, who have already held talks with club officials over a possible takeover.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Bale is said to be involved purely in an advisory role for now, but with WalesOnline claiming that the former forward is worth £150 million, he could well be involved financially in time – especially considering previous comments.

After being linked with a move to buy Cardiff City, the Wales legend stated that investing in the game was “about being patient, finding the right club, and the right path for us to take,” adding that he was motivated to buy the Bluebirds because of his hometown connection to the club.

Over the summer, Bale's former team-mate Sergio Ramos reached an agreement with an investment group to take over Sevilla – an outfit that he spent two spells with – with a consortium looking to acquire a controlling stake and take on the debt of the club.

This deal fell through towards the end of May, however, with reports of terms shifting mid-negotiation and Ramos denying any bad faith.

Sevilla didn't spend a single penny improving their squad during the 2025 transfer window, making free signings and collecting fees for the likes of Dodi Lukebakio and Loic Bade, before making a net profit again this summer, with their biggest buy, Scottish striker Robbie Ure, for around £5m.

After finishing 13th last term, the Rojiblancos are currently 13th in the table and hosting a Seville derby this weekend.

#992. Robertson makes history with record 103rd Scotland cap

Andy Robertson became Scotland's most-capped men's player with start against Switzerland in Nations League; he passed Kenny Dalglish's record of 102 caps; Robertson on Sir Kenny: "I don't want to forget and I don't want people to forget how important this man has been for our country."

Andy Robertson has broken the record for the most senior Scotland men's team caps, surpassing the feat held by Sir Kenny Dalglish for 40 years.

The Scotland captain made his 103rd appearance for the national side in Monday's 4-0 defeat to Switzerland in the Nations League.

He has bypassed the record set by Dalglish, who earned 102 caps between 1971 and 1986.

Before hitting the milestone, Robertson insisted he will always regard Dalglish as "the greatest".

"We've had so many great players for Scotland, but for me Kenny will always stand on top and I don't think that will change," the 32-year-old said.

"I don't want to forget and I don't want people to forget how important this man has been for our country."

Asked about what he told Robertson before the game, Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli said: "I just tell him that he has to enjoy it and after it's just a bonus for the future. So he needs to enjoy, to play with freedom.

"He has a lot of experience, so I don't need to tell him, but again, we are really proud of what we are living together with him. And the best way to have a good feeling for him is to have a good game."

Scotland midfielder Lewis Ferguson added: "It's amazing. First and foremost what a person, what an unbelievable captain, what a player and what an incredible servant for Scotland.

"It's a massive achievement, he should be so proud of himself and we're all just glad to be a part of that journey."

Andy Robertson spoke to BBC Scotland after the defeat in St Gallen:

"First half we were in the game but lost a stupid goal. But I thought we had chances and should have made it one each at half-time.

"We talked about it at half-time, we told ourselves to keep going and the time you get to 50 minutes, you're 3-0 down? That cannot happen in international football.

"That's what happened tonight. We were playing against a good team. But while we were in the game in the first half, you have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down, it's a tough place to come and that. A really tough night for us."

"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."

Thomas Tuchel’s side are guaranteed a place in the last eight after an impressive run including beating world champions Spain to top the group

England produced a statement win over world champions Spain in Madrid in their Nations League decider to top Group A3.

The Three Lions had already confirmed their place in the quarter-finals in March with victory over Croatia earlier in this window.

But England have now given themselves the best chances of a favourable draw by beating Spain 3-2, while also proving they are one of the teams to beat.

Thomas Tuchel’s side will be glued to next Friday’s draw, with League A still to be completed across the international break.

But here’s everything you need to know about the next stages of the competition:

The draw will take place at 11am GMT on Friday 20 November.

England will feature in the last eight of the Nations League 2026/27, with a two-legged tie to decide who will play in the semi-finals and final, both to be played across a ‘finals’ week.

As well as the Nations League quarter-finals, the League A/B and League B/C promotion/relegation play-offs will be drawn, set to be held in March 2027. The final tournament is scheduled to take place across 9–13 June 2027.

England's potential opponents in the last eight of the Uefa Nations League, as things stand, are Belgium, Netherlands or Denmark.

Beating Spain ensured the Three Lions will face a second-placed team in their quarter-final; Belgium have finished second in their group, while Germany thrashed the Netherlands to condemn the Dutch to runners-up. Denmark need a point against Norway to secure second-place.

England topping the group also means they will play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.
