#942. Alcaraz dominates Tiafoe in ATP Finals opener to extend winning streak

Is this the week Carlos Alcaraz gets his hands on the Nitto ATP Finals trophy? He dispatches Frances Tiafoe with Daniil Medvedev and Flavio Cobolli to come in round-robin play; You can watch the ATP Finals in Turin this week on Sky Sports Tennis

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Carlos Alcaraz powered past Frances ‌Tiafoe 6-2 6-2 in just over an hour at the ATP ‌Finals on Monday to stretch his winning run to ​10 matches.

The Spaniard is aiming for his third straight title after lifting trophies in Vienna and Paris.

He's also aiming to claim the title at the season-ending tournament for the first time after losing last year's championship match in Turin to Jannik Sinner .

Sinner, the two-time defending champion at the ATP Finals, ended his season early due to a right knee injury.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tiafoe's baseline game was no match for Alcaraz's power and movement, with ​the world No 3 dominant from ‌the start.

Alcaraz has won three titles since returning to the tour at the US Open after a ​break of nearly five months due ⁠to a wrist injury.

The 2025 ⁠finalist quickly charged into a 4-0 lead as the American world ‌No 8 was left looking helpless against Alcaraz's versatile play.

In a near-flawless first set, ‌the Spaniard won 93 per cent of points on his first serve and a perfect 100 per cent on his second.

Before Tiafoe, making his ATP Finals debut, had time ⁠to react he was down a set ​and a break after half an ​hour.

He did earn three break points at ​3-2 but could not make them count ⁠with Alcaraz holding and breaking again after a superb rally and down-the-line winner to make it ⁠5-2. He served out the ​set in the next game.

"I would say this is the best I have felt so far in my career at this part of the season," Alcaraz said.

"I have never experienced something like this, this year. It was unusual for me, having a lot of months off the competition at home. So coming here I have a lot of energy and ambition and I am hungry for more."

"I tried to push him and let him know it is going to be a really great battle if he wants to win," Alcaraz added. "I am just really happy to start the tournament like this and hopefully I can keep it going."

Tim Henman, speaking on Sky Sports: "Alcaraz showed why he is the best and most exciting player in the world right now. Tiafoe will have to go away, lick his wounds and try to respond at this next opportunity.

"Just another incredible performance to marvel at. All aspects of Alcaraz's game firing on all cylinders."

On taking a step back in his schedule, Jamie Murray said: "Alcaraz has been quite vocal about the schedule and how he might miss more time on the tour to be fresher for the bigger tournaments.

"He is right because the calendar is so congested. The move to 12-day Masters events means players are away more, it's more mentally demanding - maybe more so than physical and he feels like he doesn't have to play every week of the year.

"He's going to decide what the biggest tournaments are for him and then he's going to try and peak for them."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former champion Daniil Medvedev defeated home favourite Flavio Cobolli 7-6 (7-4) 6-3 in the other group match on Monday evening.

"I managed to serve well," said Medvedev. "It's a very fast indoor court, so the serve is important. He managed to [serve] well in the break points in the first set.

"There was one point where I could have done a tiny bit better, but other than that he was serving well. I'm happy I managed to stay tough and get the win."

The fourth-seeded Medvedev will next face Alcaraz on Wednesday, while Cobolli will look to continue his quest to join Matteo Berrettini, Jannik Sinner and Lorenzo Musetti as the only Italian men to record a singles victory at this event when he next faces Frances Tiafoe.

#941. Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson

Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

#940. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

#939. The 'eclipse of the century' will plunge these 8 wonders of the Roman Empire into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027

Ancient Roman cities, temples and amphitheaters across the Mediterranean will fall into the moon's shadow during the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities.

From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east

Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene.

Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Few eclipse locations can offer two civilizations in the same photograph. Málaga's Roman Theatre was built in the first century B.C., when the city was part of the Roman province of Hispania, and today sits directly beneath the Alcazaba, the imposing Muslim-era palace-fortress that dominates the hillside above. Although its totality is considerably shorter than locations farther south, the photographic possibilities are compelling. From a carefully chosen position, it may be possible to frame the darkened sun with the theater's ancient stonework and the walls of the Alcazaba rising behind it. Another major advantage for eclipse chasers is that this extraordinary historical setting sits in the heart of Málaga, making it one of the most accessible ancient sites on the path of totality.

Start of totality and duration: 08:45 a.m. GMT; 4 minutes, 51 seconds

Altitude of sun: 38 degrees above east-southeast

Long before the Romans arrived in northern Morocco, Tamuda was already a thriving Mauretanian settlement. Founded around the third century B.C. in the Martil Valley, near modern Tétouan, the Romans established a fortified military camp here in the first century A.D., whose massive stone walls remain the defining feature of this archaeological site. Tamuda combines long totality, promising weather and an atmospheric archaeological foreground — yet remains far less famous than the Roman sites across the Strait of Gibraltar.

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Few places in the 2027 path of totality combine ancient architecture and long totality quite like Timgad. Founded around A.D. 100 as the Roman colony of Thamugadi, this remarkably well-preserved city sits on an open plateau at the foot of Algeria's Aurès Mountains. Its grid of streets, forum, theater, temples, baths and columns survives alongside its most famous monument, the three-arched gateway traditionally known as the Arch of Trajan. A relatively high sun will make close architectural compositions challenging, but Timgad's wide-open site provides plenty of possibilities for carefully planned wide-angle images.

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Just 12—15 miles (20—25 km) west of Timgad lies its military counterpart. Lambaesis was the principal base of Rome's Legio III Augusta, the legion that helped secure Rome's African Empire. Rather than an entire gridded colonial city, the attraction here is monumental military architecture, most notably the imposing remains of the heart of the fortress. The eclipse circumstances are almost identical to nearby Timgad, with more than five minutes of totality and historically excellent prospects for clear skies. Scout both sites beforehand, study where the sun will stand above the ruins, and decide which offers the strongest alignment — and the easiest access — on eclipse morning.

Start of totality and duration: 10:02 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 2 seconds

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 50 degrees above east-southeast

Djémila trades a long eclipse for one of the most spectacular settings on the path of totality. Known to the Romans as Cuicul, this exceptionally well-preserved city was built in mountainous terrain around 2,950 feet (900 meters) above sea level — an unusual setting for a Roman settlement — and its ruins include temples, forums, houses, baths, arches and a theater. The surrounding green hills and mountains give eclipse photographers a very different backdrop from the flatter, more arid landscapes farther south. The catch is totality, which is significantly shorter than at other Roman ruins.

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 19 seconds

Altitude of sun: 54 degrees above east-southeast

Sbeitla could be one of the great archaeological settings for the 2027 eclipse. Known in Roman times as Sufetula, the city prospered under Roman rule and today contains some of Tunisia's most impressive ancient ruins. Its centerpiece is an unusual group of three remarkably well-preserved temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, standing above the forum and reached through the monumental Arch of Antoninus Pius. That high sun will require some careful positioning and probably a wide-angle composition, but eclipse photographers will have an extraordinary collection of arches, columns and temples to use as foregrounds.

Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes, 23 seconds

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 56 degrees above east-southeast

It may be the third-largest and one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters in the world, but El Jem offers another reason to consider it for totality. Unlike Rome's Colosseum — which it closely resembles — visitors can explore its multi-tiered seating, climb high into the surviving structure for panoramic views and visit the underground passages once used by gladiators and animals. Built around A.D. 238, El Jem combines one of Rome's greatest surviving monuments with some of the most promising eclipse conditions on the entire track.

#938. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#937. Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain

As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart

Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Those within the Scotland setup regard Robertson as the glue who holds the scene together, a decorated footballer who treats everybody the same and carries out an abundance of unseen work to make this team better. Robertson has routinely paid for squad nights from his own pocket.

The 32-year-old is as dedicated to overall environment as he is to his craft. Under Robertson’s on-field guidance, Scotland have morphed from international also-rans to serial tournament participants.

Left-backs are rarely the recipients of praise. When of the status of Robertson they do, however, receive criticism when a team struggle. He has carried the heaviest load while probably unable to celebrate the highs in an appropriate manner.

Robertson’s journey sets him apart and not only from Dalglish. By March 2014, when Robertson made his debut as a 67th-minute substitute in a friendly in Warsaw, he had been rejected by Celtic’s youth system, reset his career at Queen’s Park and turned heads in Dundee United colours. Hull would come next.

“He counts as one of my best-ever signings,” says Steve Bruce, who took Robertson to Humberside. “I still remember him holding his parents’ hands when he came down.

“He could run like the wind and had such a lovely left foot. We wanted to try and sign the best young players and thought he might get a few games due to injuries but Andy went into the side and never came out, which is testament to him. I’m absolutely delighted for him.”

Robertson and Phil Bardsley replaced Alan Hutton and Barry Bannan in Poland. “He was a young boy who played with so much freedom,” Hutton says. “He had energy and aggression to go up and down the pitch all day long, he would shell crosses into the box at 100mph. For one so young, he was also amazingly good at one v one defending. I got to 50 caps. I remember thinking there would be no chance of anybody reaching 100.”

Alex McLeish, who handed Robertson the Scotland captaincy in 2018, jokes about the possible impact on Dalglish. “Kenny will want to make a comeback,” he says. “No, he will be absolutely delighted for Andy. It tells you so much about Andy’s character that someone like Kenny Dalglish is so fond of him.

“It felt to me like a new era. We were rebuilding and Andy seemed to make the most sense as being at the forefront of that. I’m pretty sure anyone else would have made the same decision. A fantastic player with a great attitude and very well liked by all his teammates. He was a natural captain. He demands high levels without being someone to blast people. He is a hard bugger; if he talks, people shut up and listen.

“When I told him [he was captain], I still remember how his eyes lit up. He loved hearing that. He gave me such a great big smile and said how honoured he would be to captain the country.”

McLeish underplays the value of his decision. Robertson has worn the armband 80 times. McLeish could easily, for example, have handed it to Kieran Tierney, Callum McGregor or John McGinn. McLeish’s faith in Robertson and convincing of Scott McTominay to commit to Scotland were huge and lasting contributions.

Robertson’s career could easily have followed an alternative path. The Scottish game is laced with players released by major clubs who spend years lurching about in its nether regions. Blair Spittal, who played with Robertson at Queen’s Park and Dundee United, believes there may be a broader lesson here. “I’m not saying every player could do the same as Andy, but within the pyramid of Scottish football there are definitely players who just need an opportunity and someone to show their belief,” he says.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“Queen’s Park at the time was a great environment for that. We were then very lucky at Dundee United to have a manager [Jackie McNamara] who believed in young players. Andy took everything in his stride. Nothing ever fazed him.”

He has made instant impressions everywhere. John Rankin was a senior player at Dundee United as Robertson elevated his reputation. He recalls a pre-season friendly at Union Berlin, when he first clapped eyes on someone who would be a Champions League winner within six years. “Who is this?” Rankin said while watching from the stand. “On his first day at the training ground, Andy bypassed the first‑team dressing room to get changed with the youth team. He was so unassuming, no entitlement about him at all.

“He knew what he wanted to do. On the pitch it was a case of: ‘Get out my road, I’m coming through.’ Off the pitch he was such a humble guy, who knew his life was built on the hard work of his parents. He had hunger to be the best player in every single session. It was never about being flash, it was about working his way to the top.”

During a game at Motherwell, with United 3-0 up, Rankin warned teammates to remain compact. Next came a marauding Robertson, who cracked home a fourth before Rankin chastised him for not following orders. “But I scored, didn’t I?” came the retort.

Jordan Henderson and James Milner have been hugely influential in shaping how Robertson deals with others. Robertson did not want Steve Clarke to call time on his Scotland managerial career in June, but during an emotional meeting in Charlotte it was clear the latter’s mind was made up. Clarke would not have returned to Hampden Park four months later but for Robertson, who was receiving recognition for 100 caps.

It is fortunate Dalglish is not protective of his record. McGinn entered this international break with 93 caps. Ryan Christie and McTominay have an outside chance of reaching 102. Billy Gilmour is 25, but hit 50 caps in October. “It’s not about now holding on to the record for ever,” Robertson says. “That’s not really me.”

Modesty. A consistent and endearing Robertson trait. Whenever this international career for the ages ends, he will be a monumental loss.

#935. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

#933. I used the Vaonis Vespera 3 for weeks and here’s who I would recommend it to — full review

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The Vespera III is a premium smart telescope that delivers powerful features like multi-night observation and mosaic technology, rewarding avid astrophotographers who have a serious interest in capturing the night sky.

Excellent deep-sky images with rich colors

Multi-night imaging makes ambitious targets easier

Much more expensive than many of its rivals

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes, from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro. They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer.

At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery.

That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much.

One of my favorite things about smart telescopes is watching a photograph develop as more light is collected. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment.

With the Vespera 3, I spent several nights photographing the Pleiades (M45), the famous star cluster in Taurus. The Pleiades make an excellent subject for testing a telescope because the stars are bright, but the surrounding nebulosity is much harder to capture convincingly. The Singularity app used to control Vespera 3 stacks each image as it goes, but keeps them in sight as an optional time-lapse, so you can see exactly why you’re spending so much time on one object.

Even better, the Vespera 3’s PerseverENS feature lets you add data to an existing observation over multiple nights (it’s actually called multi-night observation in the app). Instead of having to call it a night or start again every time the weather interrupts an imaging session, you can return to a target and continue building the image over weeks — or years. This is excellent for faint nebulas, but also for anyone who lives somewhere with unpredictable weather.

The Vespera 3 also has CovalENS, Vaonis’s mosaic imaging system, which captures adjacent sections of sky to produce a larger image. That’s helpful for objects such as the Pleiades and large nebulas, which occupy a substantial area of the sky.

Mosaics inevitably take longer than conventional images — if it images six sections of the night sky, it takes six times longer for the same image quality — but they also make the telescope more versatile than its native field of view (2.5 x 1.4 degrees) might suggest.

Smart telescopes are particularly useful for people living under light-polluted skies. A conventional optical telescope can show you the moon, the planets and some brighter star clusters, but faint nebulas are largely out of reach. The Vespera 3 tackles that problem by taking repeated short exposures and combining them automatically. As the exposures accumulate, faint details become clearer, and the image becomes less noisy.

I photographed the Orion Nebula (M42), one of the most rewarding deep-sky targets for almost any telescope. Its bright central region makes it a quick capture, but the surrounding clouds of gas give a camera plenty more to uncover. The color in M42 via the Vespera 3 was particularly striking: stars looked sharp, the background was pleasingly clean, but the colors had a richness you don’t always see from less expensive models.

The Vespera 3 uses a 50mm refractor telescope and an 8.3-megapixel Sony IMX585 camera sensor. Those specifications are identical to the Vespera 2, but the Vespera 3 has a new optical system, which uses four lenses in three groups, including two extra-low-dispersion elements. Vaonis has also introduced internal baffling to reduce unwanted reflections from nearby artificial lights. For urban astronomers, every little helps. I wouldn’t claim that the Vespera 3 makes dark skies unnecessary. It doesn’t — and if you do take a trip to dark skies with the Vespera 3, your images will improve — but it can produce extremely satisfying images even from a city.

For anyone who wants more control over their images, the Vespera 3 also saves lossless TIFF files that can be exported to a PC or Mac using a USB-C cable. That means you can take the images into your preferred editing software for further processing, rather than relying entirely on the results produced by the Singularity app.

There’s something wonderfully simple about looking at a map of the night sky, spotting an interesting object and tapping it to point your scope in that direction. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy using Seestar smart telescopes. I did miss that experience with the Vespera 3.

Vaonis’s Singularity app has an extensive catalog of galaxies, nebulas, star clusters and other targets, but I found myself browsing lists when I’d rather have been exploring an interactive sky chart.

There is a section devoted to constellations, which initially got my hopes up. I thought it might allow me to photograph an entire constellation, capturing its familiar star pattern as a wide-field image. Sadly not — each constellation has a diagram showing where the catalog’s deep-sky objects are located. That’s useful if you already know what you’re looking for, but it isn’t the same as being able to see the sky overhead and choose a target visually.

However, the telescope can still find and photograph the objects in its catalog, and the automated tracking works well once you’ve made your choice.

That smart telescopes give you instant gratification is something of a selling point — but it’s also a myth. Yes, they save an enormous amount of work compared with traditional astrophotography equipment. There’s no separate tracking mount to align, no camera to attach and no laptop required to control the imaging process. However, automation doesn’t necessarily mean instant results.

For example, every time the Vespera 3 is switched on, it needs to establish its position by identifying stars overhead. Its Star Zone Search and autofocus procedure took around five minutes, with a percentage displayed in the app to show how far it had progressed. That’s not an unreasonable wait for a sophisticated astronomical instrument, but it felt a little drawn-out when I was eager to begin photographing something. If there are clouds, expect it to take much longer.

Once the Vespera 3 had aligned itself, I could choose a target and leave the telescope to work. The optical arm moved into position, the camera began collecting exposures and an image gradually appeared on my smartphone.

I was less impressed by the touch-sensitive power button. Its softly illuminated indicator didn’t always make it obvious whether the telescope was switched on. More than once, I had to check my phone’s available Wi-Fi networks to establish whether it was on or off.

Vaonis claims the Vespera 3 can operate for up to 11 hours. I didn’t run it continuously until the battery was exhausted, but it lasted longer than every observing session I attempted. That did change how I used it, because I could concentrate on the target instead of keeping an eye on the remaining charge or wondering whether I should connect a portable battery.

The new, improved tripod also makes a difference. It’s tall, adjustable and reassuringly stable, with a useful canopy strung between its legs for holding any accessories — perhaps filters, a red torch or snacks.

The Vespera 3 is capable of photographing the moon and the sun, although solar photography requires a properly fitted optional solar filter. Unfortunately, that costs a further $179/£159, which is rather steep.

It’s also not the best choice for detailed planetary images. The 245mm focal length is ideal for framing many galaxies and nebulas, but Jupiter and Saturn remain small subjects.

Another omission is an equatorial tracking mode. Some cheaper smart telescopes — such as the Seestar S50 Pro and the DwarfLab Dwarf 3 — offer EQ mode for more advanced imaging, but the Vespera 3 relies solely on its motorized alt-azimuth mount. That doesn’t stop it from producing excellent photographs, but it does mean more experienced users have one less option to experiment with.

The biggest question surrounding the Vespera 3 isn’t whether it works — it’s whether it’s worth the money. After all, it costs far more than the Seestar S50 Pro, which also has built-in imaging filters, whereas the Vespera’s light pollution ($229/£219), dual-band ($399/£370) and solar (£179/£159) filters are optional purchases. They do, however, make a significant difference — with the dual-band filter giving nebulas more contrast, color and detail.

Overall, the Vespera 3 offers a slightly more polished imaging experience than the many entry-level smart telescopes on the market. I enjoyed its clean, colorful images and appreciated the ability to work on the same subject over several nights, while the excellent tripod and battery endurance make it particularly well suited to longer observing sessions.

I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone, but I can see why someone who already loves photographing the night sky might happily pay extra for the Vespera 3.

#932. Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson

Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

Magnusson: And your time starts … now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016, though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs, and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s.

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director.

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.

Which brings us to Mauricio Pochettino. He has done remarkable things: he may not yet have won trophies in England but he effected such an extraordinary transformation at Tottenham that it seemed not unreasonable they should be part of the Super League project. He found things difficult at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, but most people do. A last-16 exit at a home World Cup with the USA was about par. The question, now he is 54, is whether the sense of drift about his career is an unfortunate and temporary state, or evidence that he is not quite what he was.

Perhaps the United job will revitalise him and he will revitalise them. But this feels like another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago; that United, once again, are answering the previous question.

#931. Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe

Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding

In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: somehow, anyhow. What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too.

Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch.

As they went there was celebration for them, applause for all of them, Spain too. What a game it had been, what a night. “We knew we would beat them,” Declan Rice claimed afterwards. Would? Maybe in the 60th minute they had known, England 3-0 up and playing their way to a superb and, yes, comfortable victory over the world champions – the first team to beat them, penalties aside, in 44 games and almost a thousand nights. But with half an hour left Spain had been revived, England reduced to 10 men and, as Tuchel said: “Thirty minutes against Spain feels like three hours.”

It did to him, to his players too. To everyone else, it flew by. This is the best game you can see in football, Spain’s head coach, Luis de la Fuente, had said, and he wasn’t wrong. When England got that third, the fans had sung: “You’ve seen the England, now eff off home.” Nah, you’re all right, thanks. Far better to stay and watch this; it had been hugely impressive from England; now, here were Spain too. Now, it was going to be wild. Nervy, noisy and fun.

Jarell Quansah lost the ball, Fermín López released Lamine Yamal and Spain won a penalty that Mikel Oyarzabal scored. It was some game. Twice Spain scored; countless times they came, the Metropolitano chanting: “Yes, we can!” In the end, they could not, but they had got close. They had really believed they might; as the momentum built, perhaps they had really believed they would.

This was history: made by England, perhaps; broken by England, certainly. Spain had not been beaten in 90 or 120 minutes since Colombia defeated them two and a half years ago, their only loss in that period coming on penalties against Portugal in last year’s Nations League final. They had not lost a competitive game since Scotland in March 2023. That, Fifa said, was the longest run ever and even if there was an asterisk, it was still mightily impressive, but it had to end some time. If not necessarily like this.

“With every passing game, defeat gets closer,” De la Fuente said. Now, it arrived. “They can seem invincible but we’re ready,” Tuchel had said. At the end Spain’s staff lined up to applaud their players off. England’s players stood before their fans, exhausted, arms raised.

Italy went into their clash in Brussels top of Group A1 after their 3-1 win against France on Thursday but came crashing back to Earth as they were comfortably beaten by Belgium.

Pio Esposito gave Italy ⁠an early lead but their joy was short-lived as Belgium scored ​three times before the ​interval through Maxim De Cuyper, ​Nathan Ngoy and Jérémy Doku (pictured). Diego Moreira made it 4-1 in the 80th minute.

France beat Turkey 2-1 in Bordeaux ​thanks to an own ‌goal by Emirhan ​Topcu and ​an effort by Bournemouth's Eli Junior Kroupi, meaning they won the group with 13 points, ahead of Belgium who ended on 12. Italy, on 10 points, missed out.

England and Spain had already confirmed qualification to the quarter-finals before Sunday's dramatic clash between the sides in Madrid, which England won 3-2, but the remaining match in Group A3 saw Croatia beat Czechia 2-1, thanks to Lovro Majer's 87th-minute winner.

In Group C1, Albania sealed top spot and promotion to League B after a 2-0 win over Belarus in Budapest. Rey Manaj and Elseid Hysaj scored goals in each half. Finland ended their campaign in the group with a 7-2 thumping of San Marino in Helsinki, headlined by a hat-trick by forward Adrian Svanbäck. San Marino are relegated to League D after failing to register a single point from their six games, ending with a goal difference of -22.

In Group C2, Montenegro completed an unbeaten group campaign with a 4-1 victory in Cyprus. Genoa forward Milutin Osmajic got them off to a fast start in the fifth minute while Nikola Krstocic added a second-half double. Armenia and already-relegated Latvia played out a goalless draw in Riga. Reuters and Guardian sport

Ultimately, this came in two acts. The first act was superb from England, the second heroic. “We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us,” De la Fuente had said and yet what was so striking about the way that this began was that England took the game to Spain on their own terms. They were the ones dominating the ball, not allowing their opponents out; theirs was the midfield, the control.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Ten minutes is not a reliable sample size it is true – and it turned out even an hour might not have been enough – but as the clock rolled into double figures, the possession stat showed 70% for England. While that number fell, when it reached 20 the shot count was 4-0. The first came after 39 seconds and before Spain had a touch, Unai Simón flashing out a right hand to Jude Bellingham’s shot inside the six-yard box. Martín Zubimendi immediately had to stop Anthony Gordon’s shot and then Simón stopped Rice. All that inside three minutes; three more and Kane was flashing a shot just wide.

England’s fans were enjoying this. A chorus of “the best in the world, the best in the world, Harry Kane, the best in the world” came down. They watched England control Spain’s place, Elliot Anderson and Rice excelling. They watched England take the lead, Kane scoring his 93rd goal with penalty No 28. They watched Bellingham burst through, responding by launching into a rendition of the Beatles which was still going when they watched Ezri Konsa head in the second. Then they watched Bellingham burst through again to set up Ben White. They watched England be brilliant for an hour but there was still plenty of Spain to watch as well. Nervously now and they will remember Trafford’s superhero rescue for some time, but it was still their night, and what a night.

A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above.

Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments.

But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory.

HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range.

This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO.

So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024).

While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface.

A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

#929. Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate

Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career

It was just what they needed at just the right time. For a tricky first half and beyond, Elversberg had been a stone in Borussia Dortmund’s shoe, the promoted side not just keeping the home team at bay but keeping them honest, nourishing ambitions of their own. “The fatigue was clearly visible,” the sporting director, Ole Book, said to Sky after a week which had contained Der Klassiker in Munich and a hard-fought Champions League victory against Betis. “We were a bit too focused on managing the game, which was understandable.”

Enter Felix Nmecha. BVB have enjoyed a largely excellent start to the season, are unbeaten and level on points with Bayern Munich at the top; Bayern lead, unsurprisingly, thanks to their superior goal difference. It is a gap which has been widened by Dortmund being far from prolific, a facet which looked as if it might undercut their efforts to roll over their visitors on Saturday, especially in the absence of the injured centre-forward Serhou Guirassy.

Somebody was needed to break it open, and it was Nmecha. With two majestic sweeps of his right foot, two rockets from outside the area, he won the game for his team. His decisive moments of elevated quality pulled BVB away from their opponents when the game threatened to drift. “In terms of talent, qualities, and technique, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world,” Book beamed. “Add to that his finishing ability, and there aren’t many who are better.” That they go into the international break neck-and-neck with Bayern is all down to their No 8.

After scoring, Nmecha pointed to the sky, then mimed lifting a crown from his head and placing it on the ground. It was nothing new. He did the same, also in front of the Südtribune, the yawning, world-famous 24,000-capacity terrace in which much of the club’s hardcore support stand, after scoring against Paderborn in September. It was the same celebration that Nmecha used when he struck Germany’s opening goal of the World Cup against Curaçao.

The celebration is a nod to Ballers in God (BIG), the Christian group founded “to use the global platform of football to make Jesus known”, and in particular to their campaign The King’s Return. Yet this latest display provoked a response from BVB’s fan and support department. “When it comes to the values of our club,” it said in a statement the day after the Elversberg game, “discrimination, and the question of what kind of societal image of humanity is given space within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent.”

The German public broadcaster ARD has linked BIG to ultra-conservative positions on issues including homosexuality and transgender identity. “Footballers are role models for millions of people, especially children and young people,” the fan and support department continued. “If this reach conveys content that excludes certain groups in society, we cannot dismiss this as merely private religious practice. Where religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, our tolerance for intolerance ends.”

Reports suggest the club has been in dialogue with Nmecha since the Paderborn game, and a statement issued in response to Kicker’s inquiries said those talks would continue – while defending Nmecha. “For Borussia Dortmund, it is essential to take the concerns and needs of the fanbase seriously and to address them,” the club said. “Naturally, we also take the current media coverage and the associated questions and discussions very seriously.” Dortmund appear to have been careful not to use any images of the celebration on the club’s official social channels.

These issues and this dialogue have been almost a constant since Nmecha arrived in June 2023, as a de facto Jude Bellingham replacement. His faith had already been a key part of his social media messaging and, as his transfer from Wolfsburg neared completion, some fan groups voiced their opposition, pointing to Nmecha’s sharing of anti-trans posts by the American rightwinger Matt Walsh, among others. A bright yellow banner was hung outside Signal Iduna Park sprayed with the message “@BVB Steh zu deinen worten”, a message to the club to “stick by your words”. In June 2023 Nmecha posted: “I genuinely love ALL people and don’t discriminate against anyone.”

Dortmund’s motto, or marketing strapline, of Echte Liebe (true love), has been used in the past decade-plus to quantify exactly what makes the club special to audiences all over the world. What BVB believe elevates them is a connection with the fans, a mutual respect and understanding that goes way beyond what has increasingly become a company-customer relationship in modern times. Engaging with supporter concerns is important everywhere in German football and, arguably at Dortmund, there is a commercial imperative to visibly do so.

It was reported widely at the time of his arrival that Nmecha had a clause written into his contract that gave Dortmund the power to fine him if he made social media posts which they felt contradicted the club’s values. The club again had words with the player in 2025 after he posted a message of condolence to the family of Charlie Kirk (Nmecha deleted another post which said Kirk had “peacefully stood up for his beliefs and values”).

Hamburg 3-1 Mönchengladbach, Mainz 1-2 Bayern, Paderborn 2-2 Eintracht Frankfurt, RB Leipzig 5-2 Augsburg, Dortmund 2-1 SV Elversberg, VfB Stuttgart 1-0 Werder, Köln 1-2 Leverkusen, Freiburg 2-0 Union Berlin, Hoffenheim 2-1 Schalke

The difference now is that Nmecha, after a difficult start in Westfalen, has become one of Niko Kovac’s key players, and one of the most recognised in his position in Europe. He scored the first goal of Jürgen Klopp’s Germany tenure, and was linked with big-money moves to the Premier League last summer. So BVB must protect their present, in the sporting sense, their future, in the financial sense, and their very fabric, in terms of their continued relationship with supporters, already strained in recent years by their deal with the arms manufacturer Rheinmetall. For his part Nmecha has responded enigmatically and characteristically, quoting a Bible verse on his socials as a caption to snaps of the game. The one thing the club cannot say is that they never saw this coming.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Bayern remain on top but nothing is easy at the moment, even after their brilliant victory at Atlético in midweek. They closed out a narrow win at Mainz but Manuel Neuer was injured again, sustaining a partial ligament tear of his right foot on the day he became Bayern’s oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days, his sixth substitution in 2026. Whether he will – or should – return is now a fair question, with Jonas Urbig a ready-made replacement. Harry Kane provided assists for both goals to reach double figures in the category, his best assist return in a season already.

The mood was not helped, however, by Uli Hoeness’s latest comments on Jamal Musiala, throwing doubt on whether he can recover his best level on the programme Der Sonntags-Stammtisch. “He’s still getting paid,” the honorary president underlined. “But imagine if FC Bayern were to say what he’s capable of now isn’t what’s stipulated in the contract?”

Even if there was another combination of the El Mala brothers – Malek setting up a goal for Saïd this week – for Köln in the derby with Leverkusen, the game had already been decided then, by a typically classy intervention by Patrik Schick.

#928. WTA chair on Pegula-Andreeva hot mic incident: It's not bad for viewership

WTA chair Valerie Camillo discusses the hot mic moment at Indian Wells between Jessica Pegula and eventual champion Mirra Andreeva and the future of the body; You can watch the ATP Finals from Turin this week on Sky Sports Tennis

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

WTA chief Valerie Camillo says private comments made by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva being overheard on a YouTube livestream is "not bad for viewership".

Camillo personally apologised to Pegula, describing the broadcast of on-court conversations during a practice session at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells as "regrettable and unacceptable".

The Tour, who operated the livestream, had intended for the microphones to capture ambient sounds from the court but failed to inform participants.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

A broadcast showed the American in conversation with her coach Mark Knowles, calling the 19-year-old a "diva" and saying she has lost respect for Andreeva's coach Conchita Martinez for not calling out her behaviour.

"Someone actually asked me if we planned it or did it on purpose to draw attention to the event," Camillo told Sky Sports' lead tennis commentator, Jonathan Overend.

"I wish that we were so crafty and strategic but we can't put ourselves in any situation where we put our athletes at risk. Our number one objective as a member services organisation for our players is to protect our players.

"What Jess said is competitive banter. I don't think there was anything particularly salacious in it. But having mics lying around that aren't being properly managed is not how the WTA expects to execute and operate.

"It created a viral moment. It created a lot of dialogue. But that's not intentional and not something you should expect to see us doing in the future.

"I've had this conversation here that I come from a variety of different sports. Before joining the WTA, I exclusively worked in male sports. I worked at the NBA and majorly baseball and it's quite common for there to be competitive banter that is brought into the forefront.

"It's up to the athletes for what they feel comfortable with and what they don't. But a little drama isn't bad for ticket sales.

"It's not bad for viewership. It's not bad for commentary. That's just a reality."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Andreeva laughed off the hot mic moment and went on to defeat Pegula 6-3 6-4 on Saturday, in a match that gained an extra layer of intrigue to reach the WTA Finals title match.

She concluded a stunning week with a second victory over Elina Svitolina to win the season-ending tournament.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The WTA was forced to replace the venue for the season-ending event from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in July, which represented a major financial setback for the governing body.

The deal with the Saudi Tennis Federation (STF) included record prize money over a three-year period, but the ongoing tension between Iran and the United States made planning for the Finals more challenging, eventually forcing the tournament to move to Indian Wells in California.

The body is projecting operating losses of £17.3m ($23m) for 2026 and expects to hold roughly £11.3m ($15m) in cash by the end of the year, according to The Telegraph. Camillo remains confident of finding extra revenue streams through in-house media rights and sponsorship growth to create financial stability.

"Our ambition for the WTA Finals is equal prize money [with the men's tour]. That's our ambition, just as we expected of the Grand Slams. All of our combined 1000 events will have equal prize money in 2027," she said.

"We've been building fandom. We've been operating globally. We've been creating superstar athletes through our platform for many, many decades, and so the athletes have the opportunity not to just earn on the court, but also to control their own brands and monetise that off the court.

"WTA intends to remain in its position as number one in the hearts and minds of fans, in the mindset and investment of our sponsors, and we want to be building an even greater platform on which our great athletes can compete, not only one that they can enjoy from the ferocity of the crowd, but also one that enables them to maximise their financial opportunity to the best of our ability."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

One of the WTA revenue streams comes from selling data, match data, court feeds to data companies with the betting industry a large part of that.

British tennis star Jodie Burrage called on social media platforms to hold people accountable for sending death threats and abuse.

Burrage, who was playing her first WTA Tour match since Wimbledon last summer, received death threats and online abuse following a first-round defeat at a tournament in India.

The 27-year-old shared a raft of abusive messages sent to her Instagram account. Alongside the video, Burrage wrote: "Nice welcome back to the tour. I remember why I left."

Camillo said: "The complexity of official data to these partners is sort of an industry inside thing. But the reality is that through having official partnerships, you actually can have more integrity and controls.

"If you don't have relationships with these variety of platforms, you can turn into a little bit of the wild, wild west. It's not to say that there isn't a financial element to these relationships. That would be disingenuous. Of course there is. But it does also enable us to have a partnership that leads to better controls."

One of the most anticipated fall TV series, "Blade Runner 2099," recently dropped its final neon-tinted trailer, and now we’ve finally got a handle on the plot dynamics of this dystopian thriller set in the cyberpunk world of Ridley Scott's original.

Prime Video's bold and brooding 8-episode series lands Nov. 25 as a tangential sequel to Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," unfolding some 50 years after the 2017 feature film. Now the artificial inmates are running the asylum when violent replicant uprisings flip the script, causing humanity to become second-class citizens.

"In Los Angeles 2099, Cora (Hunter Schafer) lived her entire life on the run, a chameleon forced to adopt numerous identities," states Prime Video's synopsis. "To secure a stable future for her brother, she assumes one final identity and is forced to partner with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Blade Runner who’s confronting the end of her life. The two are pulled into a widening conspiracy that poses an existential threat to a city that’s fighting to be reborn."

This engrossing final trailer reveals more of the detailed noir world and Cora's plight to blend into society as a Blade Runner who links up with Olwen, an aging replicant exterminator, for an uneasy partnership. Here, a tense scene plays out in this preview as Cora undergoes an intense police station screening while being used as a resistance pawn to help take back the city from usurping androids. But another deep mystery lies hidden in plain sight!

"You have to see the lie that is in front of you," warns Yeoh's dying synthetic cop.

"Blade Runner 2099" sports a spirited cast that includes Dimitri Abold ("The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes") and Lewis Gribben ("Somewhere Boy”) in collaboration with Katelyn Rose Downey ("The Nun II"), Daniel Rigby ('Renegade Nell"), Johnny Harris ("A Gentleman in Moscow"), Amy Lennox ("Only Child"), Sheila Atim ("The Woman King") and Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon”).

Delivered by creator and showrunner Silka Louisa ("Shining Girls"), and executive produced by Silka Louisa and Ridley Scott’s Scott Free Productions, "Blade Runner 2099" lands on Prime Video beginning Nov. 25, 2026.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#925. Ronaldinho makes debut for Italian side Ravenna after 11-year hiatus in playing career

Brazil legend plays first half for Serie C club at age 46

‘Is this my last one? I don’t know,’ Ronaldinho says

Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.

Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.

Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal, but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.

The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.

Ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.

“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”

Ravenna, who have not played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend’s fixtures six points behind the leaders, Spezia.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It is Ronaldinho’s second spell in Italy, albeit at a much lower level, after three seasons with Milan from 2008 to 2011, where he won one Serie A title. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona in a trophy-laden career that included claiming the World Cup with Brazil in 2002. He scored 94 goals in 207 matches for Barcelona and 33 times in 97 games for Brazil. He has also played for Brazilian sides Grêmio, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, and for Querétaro in Mexico.

#924. Number of international students arriving in US plunges — worrying scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

International students earn almost 40% of science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.Credit: Bill Pugliano/Getty

The number of international students arriving in the United States in August for the start of the academic year has fallen by 28% since 2024, reaching the lowest level since the depths reached in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Data from the federal National Travel and Tourism Office show that the number of incoming student-visa holders fell from 387,000 in August 2024 to 277,000 in August 2026 (see ‘Students stay away’). The trend has been driven by a decline in the numbers of students from India and China, which dropped by about 50,000 and 23,000, respectively, from 2024 to 2026.

Source: National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO); Nature analysis.

The number of applications from international students to US PhD programmes has also declined over the past year, falling by 21% from 2025 to 2026, according to a survey of 55 members of the Association of American Universities (AAU), a coalition of research-intensive schools.

These decreases are squeezing already strained university budgets, and researchers worry about the impact on US science. “I can’t imagine a more effective way for the US to cede its dominance in critical scientific fields to China and Europe than by reducing international students,” says Nigel Goldenfeld, a physicist at the University of California, San Diego. In 2024, international students earned 38% of the science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The administration of US President Donald Trump has introduced several restrictions on visas and international travel since Trump took office in early 2025. Last month, the administration also attempted to place a US$100,000 levy on science and engineering students enrolling in extended Optional Practical Training (OPT), a work programme used by hundreds of thousands of recent graduates and the largest pipeline of scientific talent into the United States. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposal, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”.

Federal judges have suspended the OPT charge and other efforts that the administration made to curb immigration. But higher-education specialists link these attempts to the large decrease in new overseas students, who, they say, can no longer count a US education as a stable investment. “Uncertainty has become policy, and that has registered in the hearts and minds of students,” says Chris Glass, a higher-education researcher at Boston College in Massachusetts.

The United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have also seen drops in enrolment of international students after placing new limits on these populations. But the US policies are especially restrictive, Glass says.

A spokesperson for the White House did not respond to Nature’s request for comment.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03668-x
