This Vampire Survivors spin-off has a lot of love for the famous grimdark sci-fi universe, but without the intimidatingly dense lore and complex systems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium.

Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes.

When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into.

Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos.

All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula.

If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case).

The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage.

Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core.

As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball.

Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play.

As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy.

Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures.

Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He got a BA of English Studies, focusing on English Literature, from the University of Malaga, in Spain, as well as a Master's Degree in English Studies, Multilingual and Intercultural Communication. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

#910. From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis

When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.

Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.

Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.

One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.

During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.

Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.

For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.

I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.

When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.

We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.

Michael Carrick was sacked by Manchester United this week, but the club opened talks with Mauricio Pochettino before Carrick's departure was decided or confirmed

When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.

One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.

During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.

When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!

Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.

My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.

I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.

I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.

Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.

I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.

That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.

As a player, Burrows helped third-tier Swindon Town shock Arsenal in the 1969 League Cup final. As a manager, he had spells in charge of Portsmouth, Cardiff City (both twice) and Swansea and was also assistant manager at West Brom

I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.

Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.

We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.

"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."

That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!

It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.

I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.

It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.

I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.

It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.

Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.

Gibson appointed Pulis as Boro boss in December 2017. They reached the play-offs that season, then missed out on sixth place in the Championship by a single point in 2018-19

I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.

When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.

I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.

Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.

I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.

After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.

Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.

After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.

My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.

I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.

My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

#909. Rice: More to come from Arsenal's £105m 'bargain'

Declan Rice has agreed a new long term-contract at Arsenal so can he continue to go from strength to strength? Jack Wilshere, his former team-mate at West Ham, tells Sky Sports Rice is "definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world"

Football Features Writer @nicholaspwright

Arsenal's Kroenke family owners tend not to get involved in transfer dealings but when it came to Declan Rice, and the prospect of spending £100m on a player for the first time, they needed to be sure that it was a sensible investment.

So, in the conference room at Arsenal's training ground, co-chair Josh Kroenke asked to be walked through the deal by Mikel Arteta, former sporting director Edu, then executive vice-chair Tim Lewis and now chief executive officer Richard Garlick.

"My eyebrows raised because I didn't know if we were in that phase just yet to go after a player like that," Kroenke recalled. He wanted to know what he would bring and how Arteta would use him. He wanted reassurance that he could hit the ground running.

Kroenke left the meeting in no doubt about the deal, either financially or in footballing terms. A club-record approach to West Ham was greenlit and Rice has of course gone on to prove an inspired addition, his new deal reflecting his importance.

"Declan Rice, we got him half price," is the refrain among Arsenal supporters. A player instrumental in their Premier League title success, who insisted "it's not done" then did more than anyone to drive them over the line, is now tied down for his peak years.

He has brought Arsenal even more than the club anticipated, arriving as a No 6 before being unshackled as a rampaging No 8, then reverting to a deeper role this season.

He scores, creates and dominates physically. His deadly set-piece delivery is another string to his bow.

"He is becoming a total player," said Arteta, who has even called on him at right-back. Of course, Rice filled in admirably in that role. "A total player has to be able to do as many things as possible and he has the capacity to do that," added Arteta.

Rice's adaptability and willingness to evolve his game have been themes of his time at Arsenal and the same traits were apparent to those who worked with him at West Ham, where he made an instant impression on his former team-mate Jack Wilshere.

"I love Declan, first of all a person," Wilshere tells Sky Sports. "I could see that straight away when I went in. He was very humble, his eyes were open, he wanted to learn, he would ask the right questions, and he just went from strength to strength.

"His footballing ability speaks for itself, but I wouldn't say he's someone who it came naturally to. He had to work on his right foot, on his left foot. But physically, he was always a beast and that would help him get out of certain situations."

Wilshere also noted the leadership qualities that have come to the fore at Arsenal. "Even when I went there and he was 19 or 20 and finding his way in the team, he had natural leadership and a natural aura about him that you could see," he says.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"He has a good understanding as well. When you look at players making big moves now, for me, one of the most important things around it is timing. I think Dec got his timing right.

"He spent a good few years at West Ham becoming a hero, becoming an important member of that team, trying to get that team up the table to finish high as possible. He won a trophy with them, and then he decided to go and compete for bigger things."

Wilshere and Rice crossed paths again following his move to Arsenal, where Wilshere, now head coach of Luton Town, was working as an academy coach and shadowing his old team-mate Arteta.

"I know how important he was to Mikel at that time when Mikel brought him in, and how he was going to be that shining light of the team who would always be present," he says.

"That's another thing that's really impressive about him: his robustness. He plays every single game. He dominates every single game physically."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rice's record bears it out. Last season was his most demanding yet as he made 55 appearances in all competitions for Arsenal, many of them while managing hamstring nerve pain, before making a further eight for England at the World Cup during the summer.

He is an incredible athlete who continues to show remarkable resistance to injury. He has only missed five out of 119 Premier League games since his arrival at Arsenal. Only four outfield players have played more minutes in the competition in that timeframe.

His reliability is invaluable to Arteta and Rice continues to find ways to improve. Having moved back to the base of midfield this term, switching to the right side of the pivot to accommodate Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes, he has become notably more incisive with his passes.

According to Opta, Rice ranks second among Premier League players - and top among midfielders - for line-breaking passes this season, behind only Jan Paul van Hecke. He also ranks second only to Martin Odegaard for line-breaking passes in the final third.

He is sometimes criticised for sideways passing but he is averaging nearly twice as many line-breaking passes than last season, showing clear development in yet another area of his game.

The hope for Arsenal is that Rice will continue to unlock more levels after committing his future to the club. And certainly, that is the expectation from those who know him.

"I actually think there's more to come from Dec," adds Wilshere. "I've said it for a few years now. To be fair, he has started to add goals, but I still think he can add more with his physical ability, with his ability to strike the ball off his left foot, right foot.

"But he's already a top player and definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world."

#907. SpaceX's Starship megarocket will launch to orbit on Nov. 13. Will you be able to spot it in the night sky?

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

"It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt?

Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13. Starship will fly from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area.

"As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the 'jellyfish') with the sky darker for observers further east."

If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system. Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt.

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun.

Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say.

"It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky."

Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky.

The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear.

"During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S."

Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun."

Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41.

The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. "

There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above, Star Dash, Orbital Radar and Find Starlink.

Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt.

Editor's Note: If you capture a photo of Starship and want to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#906. Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders

Voting is now open for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Listen: Who is your BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026?

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3â0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

#905. Record-breaker Robertson speaks out after Scotland's bad loss to Switzerland

Switzerland vs Scotland. UEFA Nations League Group B1.

Match report as Scotland lose to Switzerland in their final Nations League Group B1 match; Lewis Ferguson's own-goal put the hosts ahead; Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni scored in the second half; Scotland will remain in League B for the next Nations League tournament

Football Journalist @AlisonGConroy

Andy Robertson created Scotland history, then delivered a scathing assessment of their Nations League collapse against Switzerland.

On the night he became the men's record appearance holder with 103 caps, Sebastien Pocognoli came under pressure with a bruising 4-0 defeat in St Gallen.

"That cannot happen in international football," he told BBC Scotland after the match.

"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."

The Scots were comfortable against the much-changed Group B1 winners until the 22nd minute when midfielder Lewis Ferguson put through his own goal.

The unforced error deflated the visitors, who lost wing-back Aaron Hickey to injury before the break, and there was more damage in the 47th minute when Samuel Ballet's drive was touched in by Winsley Boteli before Alvyn Sanches hammered in a third just four minutes later, with substitute Zeki Amdouni adding a late fourth.

The Scots finished third in the group behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with seven points from 18, missing out on a promotion play-off spot next year and a more favourable seeding for the European Championship qualifying draw next month.

The Belgian boss' first campaign as Steve Clarke's successor has been underwhelming to say the least with just two wins - both against bottom side North Macedonia - from six fixtures and Pocognoli now finds himself under the spotlight just months into his tenure.

2: SAVE! A comfortable save for Angus Gunn but Isaac Schmidt is given too much time to get a shot away. An early warning.

17: CHANCE! John McGinn hooks the ball over the bar as Scotland continue to pile on the pressure.

22: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Disaster for Scotland as Lewis Ferguson sticks out his leg and sends the ball into his own net.

24: CLOSE! Almost an equaliser from Aaron Hickey. He gets his head to Andy Robertson's cross, but it's just past the post.

36: INJURY! Hickey pulls up holding his hamstring and his night is over.

42: CHANCE! Nathan Patterson sends the ball in to McGinn but he heads straight at the goalkeeper. An opportunity missed.

44: CHANCE! That should be a second for Switzerland! Adrian Bajrami gets on the end of the cross but somehow heads the ball well off target.

47: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Samuel Ballet plays a one-two with Remo Freuler, and Winsley Boteli gets the last touch to put the Swiss two up.

51: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Alvyn Sanches gets on the end of a ball from Boteli and fires across Gunn and into the net.

66: SAVE! Gunn pulls off a save to deny Ballet a fourth for the hosts and Luke Graham is there to block Zeki Amdouni's follow-up effort.

72: OVER! Scott McTominay gets on the end of Kieran Tierney's cross and somehow blasts it over the bar.

85: SUB! Kristi Montgomery replaces Ferguson as he makes his Scotland debut.

89: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Amdouni's shot from the edge of the box takes a deflection off Graham as it goes past Gunn.

Almost a year on from the elation of Scotland beating Denmark to reach the World Cup, it now looks like a struggle to reach Euro 2028.

Scotland will be in Pot 3 when the draw is made next month, and there is a lot of improvement needed before the qualifying campaign then kicks off in March.

In his first six games as Steve Clarke's successor, Sebastien Pocognoli has won just two. Both against North Macedonia.

They had a decent first 20 minutes in St Gallen, but this was not Switzerland's best team.

Murat Yakin was without Granit Xhaka, Dan Ndoye, Manuel Akanji and Johan Manzambi and they still made it look easy against the Scots who managed just one shot on target. A tame one.

How much time should the new Scotland head coach bet given? Following the man who led the nation to three major tournaments was always going to be a hard act to follow, but the team appears to have regressed.

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli speaking to BBC Scotland:

"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game, if I'm really honest and objective.

"I think we had some very good moments in the game, we started the game like we wanted, aggressive away from home.

"I think if we were in confidence, we would not produce the moments we produce in the game.

"I think we create good moments on the ball, on pure bravery decisions to play forward through the lines or the pressure.

"We create chances also for pressing, sometimes we should have to manage better the transition from pressing, but it is all the things we want to see.

"So the next step is to have the quality to just finish this action, and the more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things.

"We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."

Scotland captain Andy Robertson speaking to BBC Scotland:

"First half we were in the game but lost a stupid goal. But I thought we had chances and should have made it one each at half-time.

"We talked about it at half-time, we told ourselves to keep going and the time you get to 50 minutes, you're 3-0 down? That cannot happen in international football.

"That's what happened tonight. We were playing against a good team. But while we were in the game in the first half, you have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down, it's a tough place to come and that. A really tough night for us."

#903. Tenerife return to action after death of De Miguel

Tenefire fans display a banner paying tribute to Jesus de Miguel

Tenerife played their first game since the death of striker Jesus de Miguel on an emotional day at the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez stadium.

De Miguel died at the age of 30 on 3 November, a day after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a home match in Spain's Segunda Division.

Tenerife beat bottom side Ceuta 2-0 on Sunday, with tributes to De Miguel paid both before and during the game.

Lengthy standing ovations preceded and followed a minute of silence before the match.

In the ninth minute play was stopped and a round of applause took place, while a video of De Miguel was shown in the stadium, as happened at all first- and second-tier games in Spain last weekend.

Tenerife fans displayed a banner that read: "Jesus de Miguel, 9, eternally blue and white."

Forward Nacho Gil opened the scoring for the home side in the 40th minute and celebrated by holding up De Miguel's shirt.

Gil revealed a message written under his shirt that read: "Demi, always in our hearts."

Neal Viereck scored four minutes from time as Tenerife ended a run of six games without a win. They are 14th in the table.

Tenerife's game with Granada on 7 November was postponed and the club invited fans to the stadium to pay their respects to De Miguel.

Owono was given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation for the challenge which resulted in De Miguel's death.

The federation has ruled that the game between Tenerife and Andorra, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time after the incident occurred, will not be replayed and the 2-2 score will stand.

#901. Chapecoense air crash survivor wins promotion in final game

Alan Ruschel signed for Juventude in 2023

Alan Ruschel, a survivor of the 2016 plane crash that was carrying the Chapecoense football team, won promotion to Brazil's Serie A in his final game before retirement.

Ruschel, 37, was one of just six survivors when the plane crashed in Colombia and killed 71 people, including 19 of the club's players and the coaching staff.

Despite severe injuries and spinal surgery, Ruschel returned to football a year later and retires after earning promotion to Brazil's top flight with Juventude, his boyhood club which he re-joined in 2023.

Ruschel came off the bench in the 74th minute to help see out a 2-0 win over Botafogo, resulting in an emotional farewell with a lap of honour at the club's Alfredo Jaconi Stadium.

Before the game, he was also carried into the stadium on the shoulders of fans.

"I arrived here in 2007 with the club in Serie A and I am leaving the club there as well," Ruschel told a Brazilian television station after the match.

"My body wasn't responding any more. I had two consecutive knee surgeries, so I was starting to fighting with my own body.

"It wasn't working any more, even though being on the pitch was always a pleasure."

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video on social media which he posted the day before the game to confirm his retirement.

"Football has given me wonderful moments, but life has put me in front of challenges that I never imagined. November 29, 2016, a day that changed my life forever.

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye."

There were contrasting fortunes for Ruschel's former club, however, with Juventude effectively replacing Chapecoense in Serie A following their relegation after just one season in the top flight.

The club will return to Serie B having won just four games out of 34 during the season.

#900. On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years

Philae drifted and bounced around the comet for two hours before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P. To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space. The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it. Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P, all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

#899. Genetic variant that reshaped the human brain was inherited from Neanderthals

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The skulls of a human (left) and a Neanderthal (right).Credit: Philippe Psaila/Science Photo Library

A genetic variant that seems to reduce the size of brain areas involved in visual processing comes from an unexpected source — Neanderthals. People who carry the variant also have a reduced risk of schizophrenia.

Geneticists have previously found fragments of Neanderthal DNA in the genomes of many modern humans, suggesting that the two species interbred in the millennia before Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago. But this variant, described in a study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA today1, has an unusually powerful effect on brain anatomy.

“This is a very important variant,” says computational biologist Davide Marnetto at the University of Turin, Italy. “Its effect is really one of the most beautiful and strong that I’ve ever seen.”

When it comes to their brains, humans and Neanderthals have many subtle anatomical differences. Neanderthal brains were more oblong and elongated front to back, whereas modern human brains are rounder. Neanderthals also tended to have slightly larger occipital lobes — the region at the back of the brain that processes visual information.

Neanderthal-like ‘mini-brains’ created in lab with CRISPR

Neanderthal-like ‘mini-brains’ created in lab with CRISPR

In their study, evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, compared ancient DNA to data from the 1000 Genomes Project and UK BioBank, among other sources. They found evidence that a genetic variant that influences the volume of modern humans’ occipital lobes was inherited from Neanderthals.

Zeberg and Pääbo identified the variant in all five detailed Neanderthal genomes that are available to scientists, but found that it is not present in genomes of Denisovans, another extinct hominin group. In modern humans, the variant only occurs in people with non-African ancestry. It is unlikely to have been inherited from an older species that is ancestral to both humans and Neanderthals because it is found in a chunk of DNA that is 59.7 kilobases long — too big to have survived for hundreds of thousands of years.

“This is a piece of DNA that looks like it comes from Neanderthals,” says Zeberg.

The variant itself is a deletion of four nucleotides on chromosome 14 and was originally identified in 20192. Its effect on people’s brains is the opposite of what might be expected, say Zeberg and Pääbo. Even though Neanderthals had larger occipital lobes than humans do, this Neanderthal-derived variant is associated with a decrease in the volume of a part of the occipital lobe called the cuneus. Each copy of the variant was associated with 0.85 cubic centimetres less volume — an effect on the cuneus larger than any other known variant.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03762-0

Zeberg, H. & Pääbo, S. Proc. Natl Acad. Sci. USA 123, e2624837123 (2026).

#898. Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Arsene Wenger had considered running for the Fifa presidency

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger has decided not to stand against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in Fifa's presidential election.

The Frenchman had been considering running for the job but sources have told BBC Sport that he has ruled himself out.

Current world football chief Infantino's position was plunged into crisis by a backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Wenger - who is Fifa's head of global development - would have had the backing of European football's governing body Uefa, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino.

On Saturday, French newspaper L'Equipe reported that Wenger was unlikely, external to challenge his boss.

Wenger has credibility throughout the footballing world, and this will be a significant boost to Infantino as he seeks a fourth term as president.

Uefa is said to still be hopeful of finding an alternative candidate before Wednesday's deadline.

One influential figure in the group of stakeholders opposed to Infantino told BBC Sport the news was "a real shame".

"Even if not perfect, I do think he could have galvanized many around the world," they added.

Infantino laughs off resignation questions

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

However, sources have told BBC Sport that the 68-year-old has not yet secured the necessary five endorsements from member associations ahead of Wednesday's deadline but is "still fighting hard".

Amid the fallout over FFE, Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said at the time.

"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Infantino has retained support in South America, Africa and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.
